anchor_text: we'll have corn at our own price
summary: Corn (grain — principally wheat and barley) was the staple food. The citizens want the Senate to fix affordable prices rather than letting patrician grain merchants set the rate. Shakespeare wrote Coriolanus around 1608, just after the Midlands Grain Riots of 1607, when enclosures and a run of bad harvests drove up prices and provoked plebeian unrest very similar to this opening scene.

anchor_text: patricians good
summary: Patricians were Rome's hereditary aristocracy — the families who monopolized the Senate, the great priesthoods, and, until the Conflict of the Orders, the consulship itself. Plebeians (commoners) were the lower citizen class who could vote but were long excluded from high office. This gap between 'patricians' and 'poor citizens' is the play's defining political fault line.
detail: The strict legal divide between patricians and plebeians shaped the early Roman Republic: patricians controlled land, law, and religion; plebeians paid taxes and fought the wars but had little political voice until they won the tribunes (494 BCE, per Livy 2.32-33) and eventually the consulship (367 BCE). Coriolanus is a play about those first, contested steps toward sharing power, and First Citizen's 'the patricians good' drips with sarcasm — good for themselves, not for us.

sources.name: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita
sources.citation: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 2.23-35 (the patrician-plebeian conflict and grain shortage of the early Republic).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 11

anchor_text: leanness that afflicts us, the object of our misery, is as an inventory to particularize their abundance
summary: First Citizen's argument is compressed and bitter: their hunger is an itemized catalogue ('inventory') of how much the patricians have. The thinner the plebeians grow, the more they prove what the wealthy are hoarding. 'Particularize' means to list item by item, as a merchant's inventory does.

anchor_text: revenge this with our pikes ere we become rakes
summary: A 'pike' was a long thrusting spear — the common soldier's weapon — and also a tool with a pointed head. 'Rakes' are garden implements whose thin tines suggested a skeleton. First Citizen means: act now with weapons before starvation wastes us to scarecrow-thin sticks. The double meaning of 'pike' (weapon / implement) sharpens the threat.

The pike (weapon) / rakes (thin implements / starved bodies) double meaning is a standard gloss on this line; the physical-starvation sense of 'rakes' as gaunt bodies is well attested and textually coherent.

anchor_text: he did it to please his mother, and to be partly proud; which he is, even to the altitude of his virtue
summary: First Citizen strips Marcius's military glory down to two motives: pleasing his domineering mother, Volumnia, and feeding his own pride. The phrase 'altitude of his virtue' is biting irony — 'virtue' here means excellence and prowess, but 'altitude' implies it towers so high it has become a fault. The diagnosis of Volumnia's role is directly from Plutarch, who stresses she shaped every aspect of Coriolanus's character.
detail: Plutarch writes that Coriolanus 'was so courteous and loving to his mother, that at her desire he tooke a wife' and that she effectively formed his identity as a soldier. Shakespeare sharpens this into a psychological portrait: a grown man whose entire public self — valour, pride, contempt — is an offering to an absent mother. The charge that great deeds done from pride rather than public spirit are not truly virtuous is a classic Stoic critique (Cicero, De Officiis 1.14).

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 1-4, trans. Thomas North (1579): Coriolanus's upbringing by Volumnia.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 28

First Citizen's two-motive analysis (mother/pride) at TLN 26-29 is accurate to the text; the Plutarch source for Volumnia's shaping role is correctly cited; describing this as 'biting irony' on 'altitude of his virtue' is a defensible mainstream reading — the excess of virtue becoming fault is the play's central psychology.

anchor_text: to the Capitol
summary: The Capitol (the Capitoline Hill) was the political and religious center of Rome — the site of the great Temple of Jupiter and the Senate house. It is where Roman authority literally lives, and the place the hungry crowd is threatening to storm. Shakespeare uses it throughout the play as the symbol of patrician power.

sources.citation: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 1.55-56 (the Capitoline hill and the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, dedicated 509 BCE).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 35

The Capitol as Rome's political and religious center is historically accurate; the note that the crowd threatens to storm it is a fair reading of TLN 34-35 ('to the Capitol!').

anchor_text: poor suitors have strong breaths; they shall know we have strong arms too
summary: A bitter pun: petitioners ('suitors') who importune the powerful are proverbially said to be 'strong-breathed' — i.e. they stink, they are low, they press too close. First Citizen turns the insult back: yes, we have bad breath (we're hungry), but we also have strong arms. The plebeians reclaim a classist slur as a show of physical force.

The pun on 'strong breaths' as a classist slur against petitioners (bad breath / closeness / lowness) reclaimed as physical threat is a sound reading of TLN 44-45; the turn from social insult to assertion of force is clearly present in the text.

anchor_text: You are transported by calamity Thither where more attends you
summary: 'Transported' here means carried away, taken out of yourself by strong feeling — not 'travel.' Menenius says the citizens are so overwhelmed by their distress that they are being swept toward an even worse fate ('where more attends you'), i.e. the violence and punishment that will follow if they attack the state.

anchor_text: make edicts for usury, to support usurers; repeal daily any wholesome act established against the rich
summary: Usury was lending money at interest — technically illegal in the early Roman Republic and condemned in Shakespeare's England. First Citizen accuses the patricians of rigging the laws: making rules that protect moneylenders (useful to the wealthy) while repealing laws that protected the poor. The charge maps directly onto Elizabethan and Jacobean debates about enclosures and interest laws.
detail: Roman law at various periods (notably the Twelve Tables, c. 450 BCE) capped interest rates; lenders repeatedly found workarounds. In Elizabethan England usury debates were fierce: an Act of 1571 legalized moderate interest (up to 10%), which Puritans and traditionalists resisted. Shakespeare's audience would hear the Roman complaint as a contemporary one.

The charge that the patricians rig laws to favor moneylenders while strangling the poor (TLN 64-67) is accurately glossed; the Elizabethan usury-debate resonance is mainstream and defensible.

anchor_text: To stale't a little more
summary: 'Stale' means to make stale, to wear something out by overuse or repetition — not 'old food.' Menenius is being self-deprecating: the fable is old and he'll make it even more worn by retelling it. The word could also suggest making it trivial ('mere stale'), carrying a hint of self-mockery.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'stale' v. 2: to make stale or trite; to render common or hackneyed. Cf. Hamlet 2.2: 'the hearers... stale and unprofitable.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 74

'Stale' as make trite or hackneyed is the correct sense at TLN 74; the self-deprecating tone is right — Menenius knows the fable is old and says so; the gloss does not over-read.

anchor_text: There was a time when all the body's members Rebell'd against the belly
summary: Menenius tells the ancient fable of the Body and the Belly: the limbs once refused to feed the idle-seeming stomach, not realizing that the stomach digests food and distributes nourishment to every part. The moral is that the Senate (belly) provides for everyone even if its labor is invisible, so the people (limbs) should stop rebelling. The fable is drawn directly from Livy and Plutarch's account of the first plebeian secession of 494 BCE.
detail: The Belly fable appears in Livy (Ab Urbe Condita 2.32) as the means by which the historical Menenius Agrippa ended Rome's first great plebeian walkout. Plutarch retells it in the Life of Coriolanus (chapter 6). The 'body politic' — the idea that the state is like a living organism whose parts must cooperate — was a Renaissance commonplace; Shakespeare complicates it by letting First Citizen interrupt Menenius and actually tell part of the fable himself, showing the people know the rhetoric already and are not persuaded.

anchor_text: through the cranks and offices of man, The strongest nerves and small inferior veins
summary: 'Cranks' are narrow winding passages — here the body's own channels. 'Offices' are rooms assigned to specific functions, here anatomical chambers. 'Nerves' in Elizabethan usage meant sinews or tendons, not the modern nervous system. Menenius is describing blood and nourishment moving through every winding tube in the body — a surprisingly accurate early modern physiology.

anchor_text: I can make my audit up, that all From me do back receive the flour of all, And leave me but the bran
summary: The belly's defence is a brilliant mixed metaphor of accounting and milling: 'audit' is a financial reckoning (proving the books balance); 'flour' vs 'bran' is the result of milling wheat — fine white flour goes to the people, the coarse, low-value bran stays in the belly. The Senate, Menenius implies, keeps only the waste while distributing all the good. It is clever patrician rhetoric, and First Citizen's response — 'how apply you this?' — shows the crowd is not fully sold.

anchor_text: great toe of this assembly
summary: Menenius extends the body-politic fable to deliver a direct insult: First Citizen, who led the riot, is the body's 'great toe' — lowest and most forward, pushing ahead because he is worst ('rascal') in blood (rank). 'Worst in blood to run' puns on poor lineage ('low blood') and on a sore, infected toe ('blood' = humour). It is a calculated put-down: the man shouting loudest is the body's most degraded extremity.
detail: The great-toe extension is not in Plutarch or Livy; it is Shakespeare's addition, and it turns Menenius's conciliatory fable into a piece of social ridicule — revealing the patrician condescension beneath the diplomatic performance. 'Rascal' in Shakespeare often means lean, inferior livestock as well as a scoundrel.

anchor_text: Where he should find you lions, finds you hares; Where foxes, geese
summary: Marcius uses chiasmus and animal contrasts to demolish the crowd: where a soldier needs lions (courageous fighters), you turn out to be hares (cowardly); where he needs foxes (cunning supporters), you are geese (stupid and honking). The argument is that the citizens are useless in both bravery and intelligence — the two qualities a political faction needs.

summary: 'Garland' means a crown of flowers or leaves worn as an honor, and by extension the person you most honored or celebrated. summary: A 'quarry' in hunting was the heap of slaughtered deer or other game piled at the end of the hunt. 'Quarter'd' means cut into quarters, as a carcass is butchered.

anchor_text: Five tribunes, to defend their vulgar wisdoms
summary: Marcius announces that the Senate has conceded to the plebeians' demand: five tribunes, elected by and from the people, to protect them against patrician power. 'Vulgar' meant 'common, of the common people' — not necessarily obscene; Marcius uses it with contempt to mean 'low, common-herd judgment.' This grant of the tribunate is the historical moment Livy places in 494 BCE.
detail: Plutarch (Life of Coriolanus 7) names the first five tribunes; Shakespeare names two — Junius Brutus and Sicinius Velutus — who become the play's chief anti-Coriolanus manipulators. The tribune Brutus here is not the Brutus of Julius Caesar but a different man whose name is a coincidence of Roman history.

'Vulgar' as 'of the common people' (not obscene) with Marcius's contemptuous tone is the correct reading at TLN 207; the historical note on the 494 BCE tribunate and Plutarch's naming of the first five tribunes is accurate.

anchor_text: the Volsces are in arms
summary: The Volsci were an Italic people of central Italy who fought Rome repeatedly through the fifth century BCE. Their mobilization here is the play's first pivot: internal class conflict is suddenly displaced by external war, and the crowd's anger at Marcius is immediately defused by the news. Marcius's response — 'I am glad on't' — shows he prefers war to domestic politics.

sources.name: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 218
Livy 2.33-40 covers the Volscian wars of the early Republic (c. 494-490 BCE) and is a real and supportive citation for the Volsci as Rome's recurring fifth-century enemy.

The Volsci as an Italic people who repeatedly fought Rome in the fifth century BCE is accurate; the reading that the war news immediately defuses the crowd's anger, and that Marcius's 'I am glad on't' reveals his preference for war over domestic politics, is well supported by TLN 218-219.

anchor_text: The present wars devour him: he is grown Too proud to be so valiant
summary: Brutus the tribune delivers a sharp paradox: Marcius is too proud to be as brave as he is. The logic is that excessive pride undermines or negates the virtue it attaches to — his valor becomes something to dismiss ('mere warrior') because it is drowned in arrogance. The claim is political strategy, not accurate psychology, but it sets up the tribunes' long campaign against Coriolanus.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 14-16, trans. Thomas North (1579): the tribunes' campaign against Coriolanus's contempt of the people.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 262
Plutarch Life of Coriolanus chapters 14-16 do cover the tribunes' campaign against Coriolanus, his contempt of the people, and the senate confrontation; the citation range is accurate and supportive.

Brutus's paradox at TLN 262-263 — too proud to be so valiant — is accurately read as political strategy rather than accurate psychology; the annotation correctly identifies it as setting up the tribunes' campaign.

anchor_text: brought to bodily act ere Rome Had circumvention
summary: 'Circumvention' here means prior knowledge or the act of getting ahead of a plan by discovering it first. Aufidius is saying that Rome has learned of every Volscian scheme before it could be put into action ('brought to bodily act').
detail: The word derives from Latin circumvenire, 'to come around or surround,' and in Elizabethan English it could mean either outmaneuvering an opponent or forestalling his plan by intelligence. The line establishes the play's opening crisis: Rome has a spy in the Volscian senate, making secrecy impossible. Onions (Shakespeare Glossary) records 'circumvention' as meaning 'the gaining of an advantage over another by indirect means.'

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, 2nd ed. (Oxford, 1919), s.v. 'circumvention'.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 295

Onions' Shakespeare Glossary is real and does carry an entry for 'circumvention' citing Coriolanus 1.2, but the definition Onions actually gives is 'means or power of circumventing' — the annotation's attributed quote ('the gaining of an advantage over another by indirect means') is a loose paraphrase, not Onions' language, so the cited wording cannot be verified as stated.

The reading that 'circumvention' means Rome's prior discovery of the Volscian plan — i.e., forestalling by intelligence — is supported by Elizabethan usage (Onions) and fits the scene exactly: Aufidius laments that every scheme became known to Rome before it could be executed.

anchor_text: They have pressed a power
summary: To 'press' soldiers meant to conscript or forcibly levy them for military service; a 'power' is an army or armed force. The letter reports that Rome has already raised a conscript army, though its destination is unknown.
detail: The press (or impressment) was the standard early-modern method of raising infantry: men of eligible age were compelled into service by royal or civic authority. Shakespeare uses 'pressed' for forced military levy throughout the history plays (e.g., Falstaff's press-gang in Henry IV Part 1, 4.2). 'Power' meaning an armed force or army is common in Shakespeare; OED records this use from the 14th century. Together the phrase signals a formal military mobilization, not a skirmish.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'press' v.2, sense 4 (to impress soldiers); s.v. 'power' n., sense 12 (a military force).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 299

OED does document 'press' in the sense of military impressment and 'power' as an armed force, both with the historical range claimed; the Falstaff press-gang reference (1H4 4.2) is accurate, and the core lexical claims are well supported.

'Pressed' as forced military levy and 'power' as an armed force are both well-attested Elizabethan usages; the Henry IV Part 1 Falstaff parallel is apt, and the gloss accurately captures what the letter reports without over-reading.

anchor_text: your great pretences veil'd till when They needs must show themselves
summary: 'Pretences' does not mean false claims here; it is an older sense meaning intentions, purposes, or designs — specifically ones kept hidden. Aufidius is saying the Volscian plan was to keep their military aims secret until it was too late for Rome to respond.
detail: This is a false friend for modern readers, who associate 'pretence' with deception or a fake excuse. The Elizabethan sense, from Latin praetendere ('to hold out, intend'), means simply 'intended purpose' or 'design.' Schmidt (Shakespeare-Lexicon) cites this sense: 'design, purpose, intention.' The word carries no necessary implication of falsehood in this period, though the secrecy ('veil'd') makes the plan conspiratorial in practice.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon, 3rd ed. (1902), s.v. 'pretence' (sense 2: design, purpose, intention).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 312

Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real work with a documented 1902 Berlin edition, and it does record 'pretence' in the sense of 'design, purpose, intention' — the annotation's paraphrase accurately reflects Schmidt's second sense for the word.

The gloss correctly identifies 'pretences' as the Elizabethan sense of 'intended purposes' (not deceptive claims), and the note that it is a false friend for modern readers is pedagogically sound and textually accurate.

anchor_text: If we and Caius Marcius chance to meet, 'Tis sworn between us we shall ever strike Till one can do no more
summary: Aufidius declares that he and Caius Marcius (later surnamed Coriolanus) have sworn a private oath to fight to the death whenever they meet. Plutarch records that the two men had fought each other personally many times before and that Aufidius nursed a burning personal hatred for Marcius — a rivalry that drives the whole play toward its final confrontation.
detail: In Plutarch's Life of Coriolanus (North 1579), Aufidius is described as bearing a marvellous private hatred for Marcius because of repeated single combat between them, in which Marcius had prevailed. The oath invoked here is Shakespeare's distillation of Plutarch's portrait of Aufidius's wounded pride. This rivalry supplies the motive for Aufidius's welcome of the banished Coriolanus into his household in Act 4 and for his eventual murder of him in Act 5 -- Aufidius destroys what he cannot defeat in the field. The oath also sets up the play's central irony: the two greatest warriors of their age cannot kill each other in battle, but the political world they both despise will destroy Coriolanus in the end.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus, in The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Aufidius's longstanding private hatred of Marcius after repeated single combats.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 328

The core reading — a sworn personal combat-to-incapacitation between Aufidius and Marcius, grounded in Plutarch's portrait of Aufidius's wounded pride after repeated defeats — is mainstream and defensible; the final sentence of the detail (the political-world-destroys-Coriolanus irony) is prospective editorializing about Act 5 but does not misread the line itself.

anchor_text: picture-like to hang by th' wall if renown made it not stir
summary: Volumnia compares a man without military renown to a portrait hanging uselessly on a wall — decorative but motionless, incapable of action. The image argues that physical beauty or nobility counts for nothing without the movement and fame that war alone provides.
detail: The simile is a compressed argument for Volumnia's entire value system: a static life of domestic comfort (the bed, the embrace, TLN 338) is mere ornament, like a painting. Only action — specifically martial action — makes a man's person 'stir,' that is, come alive and matter. North's Plutarch similarly stresses that Volumnia trained Coriolanus to prize military glory above all other goods from boyhood (Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 1).

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 1, in Sir Thomas North, The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (1579): Volumnia's early ambition for her son's military honour.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 343

Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 1 (North 1579) genuinely describes Volumnia raising Marcius to prize military honour above all other goods, and the claim that his chief end was his mother's gladness in his glory is borne out in the opening chapters of the Life.

The simile is correctly parsed: 'it' refers to the person (comeliness), not the picture, and the claim that only renown makes a life 'stir' is exactly what the syntax supports; the Plutarch parallel for Volumnia's value system is apt and not overstated.

anchor_text: his brows bound with oak
summary: A wreath of oak leaves — the corona civica, or 'civic crown' — was the Roman military award given to a soldier who saved the life of a fellow citizen in battle. It was the second highest Roman decoration, worn on the head of the man honoured. Returning from a campaign with such a crown marks Marcius as already an exceptional soldier.
detail: The corona civica was made of oak and ranked just below the corona graminea or obsidionalis (the grass crown awarded for relieving a besieged army). Pliny the Elder devotes special attention to it, noting that it was peculiarly prized because it was a gift from a fellow soldier whose life had been saved, not from the commander (Natural History 16.3-5). Plutarch records Marcius winning distinctions for extreme valour from his earliest campaigns. In the play's world, Marcius will later receive a further crown and the name 'Coriolanus' for the siege of Corioli. Volumnia's detail here establishes the standard he has already set before the main action of the play begins.

sources.name: Pliny, Natural History
sources.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 16.3-5 (the corona civica, the oak-leaf civic crown awarded to a Roman soldier who saved a fellow citizen's life in battle).

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579): Marcius's early honours and decorations for valour.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 346

The corona civica identification is standard; the hierarchy (obsidionalis > civica) is correctly represented per Pliny NH 22, and the forward connection to the grass crown/surname-Coriolanus is textually grounded.

anchor_text: I had rather had eleven die nobly for their country than one voluptuously surfeit out of action
summary: Volumnia says she would rather see eleven of twelve sons die in battle than have one live in idle luxury ('voluptuously surfeit out of action'). The statement reveals the Roman patrician ideal she has drilled into Coriolanus: honourable death in service of Rome is worth more than survival in comfort. Plutarch notes that Roman mothers were expected to rejoice in their sons' military deaths.
detail: Plutarch's Life of Coriolanus opens by stressing that Volumnia raised her son with this exact value system after his father's early death, channelling her maternal feeling entirely into ambition for his honour. The word 'voluptuously' carries moral weight — a man given to physical pleasure (voluptas) is, in Stoic Roman terms, enslaved to the body and beneath contempt. 'Surfeit' (to overindulge to the point of disgust) heightens the revulsion. The speech also anticipates Coriolanus's own contempt for the Roman plebeians, who in his view prefer food and safety to martial service.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 1, in Sir Thomas North, The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (1579): Volumnia's upbringing of Marcius to prize honour above life.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 353

Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 1 and 4 (North 1579) confirm that Volumnia trained Marcius from childhood to prize honour and his mother's approval above survival, and that valiantness (virtus) was the supreme Roman virtue; the annotation's gloss on 'voluptuously' as Stoic moral condemnation is defensible but goes slightly beyond the cited source, which does not itself use Stoic framing.

The Stoic-Roman honour frame and the moral weight of 'voluptuously'/'surfeit' are correctly glossed; the generalisation that Roman mothers were institutionally expected to rejoice in sons' deaths goes slightly beyond Plutarch (who says this of Volumnia specifically), but the core interpretation of the speech is sound.

anchor_text: Like to a harvest-man that's tasked to mow Or all, or lose his hire
summary: Volumnia imagines Marcius cutting down enemies the way a hired reaper must cut all the grain in his field or forfeit his wages — total, relentless, driven by necessity. 'Hire' means his pay or wages; the simile presents warfare as a piece-work job that admits no stopping short of completion.
detail: The simile is deliberately low and practical — a field labourer paid by results — applied to heroic battle, which intensifies rather than diminishes Marcius's ferocity. Harvest similes for slaughter are common in classical epic (compare Homer, Iliad 11.67-69, where warriors fall like grain before reapers), and the image would have been vivid to Shakespeare's audience at a time when harvest failure and grain hoarding were live political grievances (the Midlands enclosure riots of 1607 are the immediate context of Coriolanus). 'Tasked' means contracted or assigned a specific task for pay; to complete it or lose the money is the pressure Volumnia maps onto her son's fighting.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 11.67-69 (warriors falling like grain before harvesters — the harvest simile for battle slaughter in classical epic).

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A., Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874), s.v. 'hire': wages, payment for labour.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 365

Homer, Iliad 11.67-69 contains the harvest-reaper simile at those exact lines (Greek: reapers driving swathes through wheat or barley in a rich man's field, with sheaves falling thick), directly supporting the claim; Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real and standard reference work.

The simile is accurately glossed; the Homer Iliad 11 parallel is mainstream in editorial commentary; the connection to the 1607 Midlands enclosure context is well-supported scholarly consensus and does not overreach.

anchor_text: the breasts of Hecuba, When she did suckle Hector, looked not lovelier Than Hector's forehead when it spit forth blood
summary: Hecuba was the queen of Troy whose son Hector, Troy's greatest warrior, was slaughtered by the Greek hero Achilles. Volumnia invokes Hecuba nursing the infant Hector — one of the most tender maternal images in the classical world — only to claim that a warrior's bloody brow in battle surpasses even that. The comparison deliberately elevates wounds above mother-love.
detail: Hecuba in ancient tradition was the supreme figure of maternal grief and of a mother's pride in a warrior son — praised in Homer's Iliad for nursing Hector, and then destroyed by watching him die and Troy fall. Volumnia's claim that Hector's blood-spitting brow at battle was lovelier than Hecuba nursing him is a shocking inversion of maternal values: what Virgilia (TLN 367, 'O Jupiter, no blood!') sees as horror, Volumnia reads as beauty. The allusion also implicitly compares Marcius to Hector — Troy's greatest champion — in Volumnia's eyes, which is a high and doomed compliment in a tragic play. Ovid, Metamorphoses 13, treats Hecuba's grief at length; Homer, Iliad 22, describes Hector's death.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 22 (Hector slain by Achilles; Hecuba's grief); Iliad 6.399-439 (Hector's farewell to wife and child — the Trojans' most human domestic scene).

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 13.404-575 (Hecuba's grief and transformation — the archetype of maternal loss used across the classical tradition).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 369

Homer, Iliad 22 covers Hector's death and Hecuba's grief, and Iliad 6.399-439 is the Hector-Andromache farewell scene (the Trojans' most human domestic episode); Ovid, Metamorphoses 13.404-575 treats Hecuba's grief and transformation — all three citations are real passages that support the claims made.

The inversion of maternal values (wounds lovelier than nursing) is the mainstream reading and correctly identified as Volumnia's deliberate revaluation; noting Hecuba's nursing is Volumnia's own rhetorical construction, not a named Homeric scene, does not undermine the gloss.

anchor_text: how he mammocked it
summary: 'Mammocked' means tore to pieces, mangled or shredded. Valeria describes young Marcius catching a butterfly, letting it go, catching it again, and finally ripping it apart in frustrated rage. The word is rare and intensely vivid — it captures the violence of the tearing.
detail: The word appears only here in Shakespeare and is otherwise sparsely recorded in early modern English. It likely derives from an intensified form of 'mam' or 'maim,' with connotations of rough, destructive handling. The anecdote is Valeria's proof that the boy is 'the father's son' — he has his father's temperament: the same relentless grip, the fury when thwarted, and the impulse to destroy what he cannot control. The episode foreshadows Coriolanus's career: a man who cannot endure resistance without turning to violence.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. Robert D. Eagleson (Oxford, 1986), s.v. 'mammock': to tear to shreds or pieces.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 392

Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, entry 'mammock' (confirmed in the Perseus Digital Library text) defines the word as 'to break into fragments,' citing exactly this passage from Coriolanus 1.3; the annotation's gloss 'tore to pieces, mangled or shredded' accurately renders the definition.

The gloss is correct and the etymology is appropriately hedged ('likely'); the thematic reading of the butterfly episode as foreshadowing of Coriolanus's intolerance of resistance is mainstream and defensible.

anchor_text: A crack, madam
summary: 'A crack' here means a lively, mischievous youngster or rascal — Virgilia is affectionately deflecting Valeria's praise of young Marcius with a mild disclaimer: he's just a naughty boy. The word is colloquial and warm in tone.
detail: In early modern English 'crack' (or 'crack-rope') was applied to a boisterous, saucy child or young person, carrying associations of mischief and high spirits rather than censure. Compare the phrase 'crackbrained' for recklessness. Virgilia's use is modest and maternal — underplaying the boy Valeria has just praised as heroically fierce. Given that the audience has just seen young Marcius described tearing a butterfly apart in rage, the mild 'crack' is quietly ironic.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. Robert D. Eagleson (Oxford, 1986), s.v. 'crack': a lively or mischievous boy, a pert youngster.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 395

Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'crack' is a real entry covering the early modern usage of 'crack' for a lively or mischievous youngster, a well-attested early modern colloquialism; the definition given in the annotation is accurate to standard lexicographic sources.

The sense (lively mischievous youngster) is correct; calling Virgilia's remark 'quietly ironic' is defensible as dramatic irony for the audience given the preceding butterfly-shredding, even if Virgilia's own intent is simply modest deflection.

anchor_text: You would be another Penelope; yet they say all the yarn she spun in Ulysses' absence did but fill Ithaca full of moths
summary: Valeria compares Virgilia's vow to stay home until her husband returns to Penelope, the wife of the hero Odysseus (Ulysses), who famously waited twenty years for him. Valeria's joke twists the comparison: Penelope's famous weaving — which she unravelled each night to delay suitors — produced nothing useful in the end but a house full of moths. It is a comic deflation of the myth to tease Virgilia out of her stubbornness.
detail: In Homer's Odyssey, Penelope kept the suitors at bay for years by promising to choose one of them once she finished weaving a burial shroud for her father-in-law Laertes; she wove by day and unravelled by night. Shakespeare's audience would have known her as the model of faithful wifely patience. Valeria punctures the ideal with a realistic objection: all that yarn, all those years, and what came of it? Just moth-eaten cloth and a house besieged by parasites. The gibe is fondly irreverent, not hostile — Valeria is trying to draw Virgilia out, not mock her. The allusion also sets up an implicit contrast between the quietly constant Virgilia and the more actively assertive Volumnia.

sources.name: Homer, Odyssey
sources.citation: Homer, Odyssey 2.93-110 and 19.138-156 (Penelope's weaving and unravelling to delay the suitors during Odysseus's twenty-year absence from Ithaca).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 409

Homer, Odyssey 2.93-110 has Antinous recount Penelope's weaving scheme to the assembly, and 19.138-156 has Penelope herself describe it to the disguised Odysseus — both passages are real and directly support the claim about the weaving and unravelling.

The comic deflation of the Penelope ideal is the right reading; the annotation slightly muddles the 'moths' joke (the suitors-as-moths resonance vs. literal moth-eaten cloth) but the overall interpretation — Valeria teasing Virgilia by puncturing the faithful-wife archetype — is sound and mainstream.

anchor_text: the Volsces have an army forth; against whom Cominius the general is gone, with one part of our Roman power: your lord and Titus Lartius are set down before their city Corioli
summary: Valeria relays the strategic situation: the Roman army has split — the general Cominius leads one part against the main Volscian force in the field, while Marcius and Titus Lartius besiege the Volscian city of Corioli. 'Set down before' means they have established a siege. This is the campaign from which Marcius will return with the surname 'Coriolanus.'
detail: Plutarch and Livy record the war against the Volscians, a recurring enemy of early Rome, and the siege and capture of Corioli (traditionally 493 BCE) as the defining event of Marcius's military career. In Plutarch, Marcius single-handedly storms Corioli and is given the surname 'Coriolanus' as a public honour by the general Cominius. The divided strategy Valeria describes — a field force under Cominius, a siege party under Marcius and Lartius — follows Plutarch's account (Life of Coriolanus 8). The audience has already seen both forces depart in Act 1 scenes 1 and 2; Valeria's news confirms the campaign is under way and brings the offstage war into the women's domestic scene.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 8-11, in Sir Thomas North, The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (1579): the siege of Corioli, Marcius's single-handed assault, and his receiving of the surname Coriolanus.

sources.name: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita
sources.citation: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 2.33 (the war against the Volscians and capture of Corioli).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 421

Plutarch's Life of Coriolanus (chapters covering the Corioli campaign, traditionally numbered around 8-11 in modern editions) confirms the divided strategy — Cominius engaging the Volscian relief force while Lartius and Marcius besiege Corioli — and Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 2.33 is confirmed to cover the Volscian war and the exploits that gave Marcius the surname Coriolanus.
Purely expository; the divided Roman strategy follows Plutarch Life of Coriolanus 8 accurately and the annotation makes no over-reading claims.

anchor_text: hear their 'larum, and they ours
summary: 'Larum is a contracted form of 'alarum,' itself from the Italian 'all'arme' ('to arms'): a trumpet call or drum signal ordering soldiers into battle. Marcius means that once the two armies are within range, they will each hear the other's battle-signals.
detail: The full form 'alarum' appears in the stage directions of this same scene. In Elizabethan military usage an alarum was both a warning call and the signal to charge; on stage a drummer or trumpeter would sound it live, bridging the action between scenes. The contracted form 'larum also survives in the modern word 'alarm.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'alarum' n., sense 1a: 'a call to arms'; 'larum, contracted form, 16th–17th c.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'alarum': 'call to arms, signal for attack.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 447
OED s.v. 'alarum' and 'larum' and Onions s.v. 'alarum' are real, standard lexicographical sources that directly support the contraction etymology and military-signal gloss.
Standard archaic-vocab gloss; 'larum as contraction of alarum is well-attested and the contextual reading (battle-signal range) matches the line precisely.

anchor_text: Now, Mars, I pr'ythee, make us quick in work
summary: Mars is the Roman god of war. Marcius -- whose very name was popularly associated with Mars -- calls directly on the war-god for speed and decisive action before the battle. The prayer is in character: Marcius worships martial violence as others worship gods.
detail: The Roman gens Marcia was an ancient patrician house, and the name Marcius was popularly linked to Mars; Shakespeare makes the connection thematic, fusing the man, his ferocity, and the divinity he invokes -- a point Cominius later elaborates in his encomium (2.2). Volumnia, his mother, has raised him specifically to embody the martial ideal. The prayer's brisk, almost peremptory tone ('I pr'ythee, make us quick') captures Marcius's impatience with anything that delays combat.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579), ch. 1: the antiquity and distinction of the house of the Marcii at Rome.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 448

Rescued in 2026-06-01 review sweep — Plutarch ch. 1 lists the distinguished Marcii but does not assert descent from Mars; trimmed the false 'gens Marcia claimed descent from Mars (Plutarch 1)' claim to the defensible 'the name Marcius was popularly linked to Mars' and re-pointed the citation to what ch. 1 actually supports (the antiquity of the house).

The invocation is in character and the interpretation that Marcius's brisk, almost peremptory tone ('I pr'ythee, make us quick') reflects his impatience with anything delaying combat is a defensible mainstream reading of his personality as established in Acts 1-2.

anchor_text: All the contagion of the south light on you
summary: Marcius curses his retreating soldiers with plague and disease. In early modern European belief, the south wind ('auster') was thought to carry infectious vapors — the very air of the south bred illness. 'Boils and plagues' are specific diseases: the plague, with its swellings (buboes), was the most feared epidemic of the age. Marcius piles disease-curses on the fleeing men, then adds that their infection should travel upwind 'a mile' so they are shunned before they are even seen.
detail: The miasma theory — that disease was carried in foul airs from warm, wet climates — was medical orthodoxy through Shakespeare's time (formally challenged only in the 19th century). The south wind's association with pestilential vapors appears in Caliban's curses ('The south-west blow on ye / And blister you all o'er,' Tempest 1.2) and in Timon ('Be as a planetary plague when Jove / Will o'er some high-viced city hang his poison / In the sick air,' Timon 4.3). The sustained disease-imagery here characterizes Marcius's contempt for the soldiers as a form of social infection.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'contagion': infectious disease, pestilential influence.

sources.name: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita
sources.citation: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 2.34 (Roman campaigns before Corioli): context for the disease-ridden army camp.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 471

Onions s.v. 'contagion' is sound; Livy 2.34 does describe a pestilence striking the Volscian army, but the annotation characterises it as 'context for the disease-ridden army camp' at Corioli, which misrepresents the passage — the plague halts a Volscian march on Rome and is not set in an army camp at Corioli.

The miasma/south-wind gloss is accurate early-modern medical orthodoxy; the reading that disease-imagery expresses Marcius's contempt for the soldiers as social infection is a defensible and mainstream interpretation.

anchor_text: From slaves that apes would beat! Pluto and hell!
summary: Pluto is the Roman king of the underworld — what the Greeks called Hades. Marcius flings the name as a profane oath of explosive fury: the Romans fled from enemies so contemptible that even apes could have beaten them. Invoking Pluto and hell simultaneously joins Roman mythology and a vernacular sense of damnation.
detail: Roman oaths by infernal deities (Pluto, Hecate, the Furies) expressed the utmost horror or disgust. Shakespeare pairs classical and Christian underworld vocabulary freely, as he does in Hamlet ('By Jove,' 'Heaven and hell') and elsewhere. Here the oath also carries an unconscious irony: Marcius, who has just driven his cowardly countrymen back into battle, is effectively ruling them through fear — a kind of infernal authority. Pluto (Greek Plouton, 'wealth-giver') governed the riches of the earth as well as the dead; his name was used for oaths expressing extreme anger or desperation.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 5.395-424 (Pluto, king of the dead); Golding's 1567 English translation was standard in grammar schools.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'Pluto': used as an oath = the ruler of Hell.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 477

Ovid, Metamorphoses 5.395-424 is a real locus (the Proserpina abduction) and does establish Pluto as king of the underworld, but the passage is about the abduction myth and does not illustrate Pluto's use as a Roman oath-word; Onions s.v. 'Pluto' covers the oath usage, so the core gloss is supportable but the Ovid citation only partially fits the stated purpose.

The core gloss (Pluto as infernal oath of fury) is sound; the 'unconscious irony' of Marcius ruling through 'infernal authority' in the detail section is an overreach not required by the text, but the summary and student-facing content are accurate and the verdict rests on the summary.

anchor_text: backs red, and faces pale / With flight and agued fear
summary: 'Agued' means afflicted with ague — a fever causing alternating bouts of burning heat and shaking chills, associated with malaria or other fevers. Marcius reads the soldiers' red backs (from exertion) and white faces (from panic) as symptoms of disease-cowardice: they sweat like fever patients and shake like ague sufferers. The image continues his disease-curse from three lines earlier.
detail: Ague (from Old French 'ague,' acute fever) was one of the most common serious illnesses in Elizabethan England, especially in marshy regions; in Shakespeare it stands for uncontrollable shaking and debility. Marcius's insult fuses two registers: the medical (these men look ill) and the moral (their illness is cowardice). The 'backs red' detail is specific: warriors with red backs were struck from behind — they ran. The contrast with 'faces pale' (turned away from the enemy) gives the image its contemptuous precision.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'ague' n., sense 1: 'acute intermittent fever ... accompanied by shivering fits and sweats'; 'agued' adj., sense 1: 'affected with ague.'

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'ague': a fever marked by shivering.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 478
OED s.v. 'ague' (acute intermittent fever with shivering) and 'agued' (affected with ague), and Onions s.v. 'ague', are real standard sources that directly support the gloss.

The reading of 'backs red' as wounds from behind and 'faces pale' as turned from the enemy is precise and well-supported; ague as uncontrollable shivering is accurate, and the continuity with the disease-curse imagery at TLN 471 is correct.

anchor_text: To th' pot, I warrant him
summary: 'To th' pot' is a colloquial phrase meaning 'finished,' 'killed,' or literally 'cut up like meat for the cooking pot.' The soldiers assume Marcius, locked alone inside a hostile city, is as good as dead. The phrase gives the rank-and-file a coarser, more darkly comic register than Marcius's heroic diction.
detail: The idiom 'go to pot' derives from slaughtering: an animal 'goes to pot' when it is killed and butchered. By Shakespeare's time it was standard slang for ruin or death. The soldiers' casual certainty that Marcius is dead contrasts with Titus Lartius's reverent eulogy in the lines that follow, and with Marcius's eventual reappearance 'bleeding, assaulted by the enemy.' The grimly comic deflation of heroism by common soldiers is a recurrent device in Shakespeare's war plays (cf. Fluellen and the leek, Henry V; Falstaff's catechism on honour, 1 Henry IV 5.1).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'pot' n.1, sense 8b: 'to go to pot,' meaning to be ruined or killed; recorded from late 16th century.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'pot': 'go to the pot, be ruined, be killed.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 490
OED s.v. 'pot' sense 8b ('go to pot,' ruin or death) is attested from 1530 (Tyndale) and Onions s.v. 'pot' is a real source; both directly support the idiom gloss.

'To the pot' as colloquial for 'killed/ruined' (from the slaughterhouse sense) is the standard reading and the note about rank-and-file deflation of heroism as a Shakespearean war-play device is a defensible interpretive frame.

anchor_text: Who sensible, outdares his senseless sword, / And when it bows stands up!
summary: Lartius praises Marcius by means of an antithesis: Marcius, who is 'sensible' (capable of feeling pain and fear), outdares his own 'senseless' sword (which cannot feel fear at all). The sword bends or breaks, but Marcius stands. The paradox reverses expected categories — the inanimate weapon is the one that yields, while the feeling man never does.
detail: The figure is an oxymoron built on the Latin root sens- (to feel, to perceive): the one who can feel suffering is braver than the one who cannot. Shakespeare uses the same paradox in Othello's 'Put up your bright swords, for the dew will rust them' and in Hamlet's comparison of himself to a soldier who 'Makes mouths at the invisible event' (4.4.50). Here it functions as the highest possible compliment — Marcius transcends matter itself. The speech closes by comparing Marcius's voice to 'the thunder-like percussion' that makes even the earth shake with fever, recalling the disease imagery Marcius himself deployed against the fleeing soldiers.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'sensible': capable of sensation, perceiving through the senses (as opposed to 'senseless,' insensate).

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 8-9 (North 1579): the storming of Corioli and the praise of Marcius's valour.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 498
Onions s.v. 'sensible' is real; Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 8-9 (North 1579) is the genuine locus for the storming of Corioli and the praise of Marcius's valour, supporting the claim.

The antithesis between 'sensible' (capable of feeling) and 'senseless' (insensate) sword is the mainstream scholarly reading and the paradox — the feeling man outdares the unfeeling weapon — is correctly identified as the rhetorical centre of Lartius's praise.

anchor_text: A murrain on't
summary: 'Murrain' was a contagious wasting disease that killed livestock — cattle-plague. Used as a curse it means roughly 'plague take it!' The soldier is furious to discover his loot is worthless base metal, not silver.
detail: The word derives from Old French 'morine' (death of animals) and appears throughout Elizabethan writing as a vigorous, rustic imprecation. Compare Caliban in The Tempest: 'A south-west blow on ye, / And blister you all o'er!' Shakespeare uses animal-disease curses to mark low social register. Here the irony is that even the looters are cheated — and Marcius arrives a moment later to despise them for looting at all.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'murrain,' n., senses 1-2: epidemic or infectious disease of cattle; as an imprecation, 'a murrain on you.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 512
OED s.v. 'murrain' senses 1-2 (livestock disease; imprecation) is standard and well-attested lexicography fully supporting the summary.

The gloss is accurate and the tone-marking claim (animal-disease curses signal low register) is a mainstream reading; the comparison to Caliban is apt though imprecise — the Caliban line given is actually a wind/blister curse, not a murrain curse, but this doesn't undermine the core interpretation.

anchor_text: crack'd drachma! Cushions, leaden spoons, / Irons of a doit
summary: A 'drachma' was an ancient Greek silver coin; 'crack'd' means it is defective and therefore worth nothing — rejected by any merchant. A 'doit' was a Dutch half-farthing, the smallest coin in circulation and a byword for trifling value. Marcius is contemptuous that his soldiers risk their lives for trash worth fractions of a penny.
detail: The two coin-words bracket the list of worthless spoils: the drachma frames the soldier with one worthless Greek coin (cracked = officially invalid), while 'a doit' dismisses the scavenged iron tools as worth less than the tiniest Dutch coin in English trade. 'Irons' here means iron implements — tools, hinges, hardware — not weapons. The contempt is characteristic: Marcius values martial honour above material gain and sees plunder as a soldier's moral corruption. Plutarch's 'Life of Coriolanus' (North 1579) records that Marcius refused a share of the spoils after Corioli, asking only for a captive Volscian who had been his host.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'doit,' n.: 'A small Dutch coin... used to express a trifling sum'; s.v. 'drachma,' n.: ancient Greek silver coin.

sources.name: Plutarch (North)
sources.citation: Plutarch, 'Life of Coriolanus,' in The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579), pp. 238-239 (Marcius refuses a tenth share of the spoils).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 514

OED entries for 'doit' and 'drachma' are correct; the Plutarch/North factual content (Marcius refusing the tenth share of spoils, asking only for a Volscian host-friend) is confirmed, but the cited page numbers 'pp. 238-239' for the 1579 North edition cannot be verified — page numbers differ across the 1579, 1595, and 1603 editions and no digitised facsimile of the first edition confirms those folios for this passage.

The coin glosses are accurate, the reading of 'Irons' as iron implements (not weapons) is correct given the list context (cushions, spoons), and the Plutarch spoils-refusal detail is directly relevant to Marcius's contempt for plunder, making the interpretation sound.

anchor_text: doublets that hangmen would / Bury with those that wore them
summary: A 'doublet' is a man's close-fitting padded jacket, the standard male upper garment of the period. English hangmen were legally entitled to keep the clothes of those they executed, but even a hangman — who would take almost any dead man's garment — would find these so filthy and degraded that he would rather bury them with the corpse. Marcius is saying the looted clothes are beneath the dignity of a hangman's perk.
detail: The hangman's right to the condemned person's clothing ('the perquisites of the gallows') was established practice in Elizabethan England, referenced in several plays as shorthand for the very lowest class of secondhand garment. The joke hinges on inversion: the hangman is supposed to be the ultimate scavenger of clothing, yet even he would refuse these. 'Doublet' was the standard English word for the fitted jacket worn over the shirt; by the 1600s it was also used loosely for any outer garment. Marcius's contempt encompasses both the physical worthlessness of the loot and the moral worthlessness of the men who would stop fighting to grab it.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'doublet,' n., sense 1: 'A close-fitting garment for the upper part of the body, originally consisting of two layers of material.'

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'doublet' and 'hangman' (the hangman's perquisites of the executed person's clothing).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 515

OED 'doublet' sense 1 is accurate; Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real and reputable reference, and the hangman's perquisite to the condemned person's clothing is historically documented in Elizabethan England.

The interpretation that even the hangman — the conventional lowest-rank scavenger of executed persons' clothes — would reject these garments is a textually grounded and mainstream reading; the inversion logic is the plain sense of the lines.

anchor_text: blood I drop is rather physical
summary: 'Physical' here means medicinal or healthful — the blood flowing from his wounds is more like a beneficial purging than a danger. Marcius is dismissing Lartius's concern: he is so fit that bleeding is good for him, not a reason to quit the fight.
detail: In early modern medicine, derived from Galenic humoral theory, controlled bloodletting ('phlebotomy') was a standard treatment for excess heat or corrupted blood. To say the bleeding is 'physical' — from the Greek 'physikos' (of nature, pertaining to medicine) — is to say it functions as a doctor's prescription rather than a wound. The word 'physician' shares the same root. This usage is common in Shakespeare: compare Macbeth 5.3 ('Throw physic to the dogs') and Hamlet 3.3. The boast also characterises Marcius: he refuses to be treated as a wounded man because that would acknowledge vulnerability and slow him down. Plutarch notes that Marcius fought on despite wounds, citing this as evidence of almost superhuman endurance.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'physical,' adj., sense 2a: 'Of or relating to medicine or healing; medicinal, curative.'

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'physical': 'medicinal, wholesome.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 529
OED 'physical' sense 2a ('medicinal, curative') and Onions s.v. 'physical' ('medicinal, wholesome') both correctly support the archaic sense claimed; the Macbeth 5.3 cross-reference is accurate.

The reading of 'physical' as medicinal/curative is the standard Shakespearean sense and the Galenic bloodletting context is accurate; the Macbeth 'physic' parallel is sound, though the Hamlet 3.3 comparison is vague and adds nothing, it does not distort the gloss.

anchor_text: fair goddess, Fortune, / Fall deep in love with thee; and her great charms / Misguide thy opposers' swords! Bold gentleman, / Prosperity be thy page!
summary: Lartius personifies Fortune as a goddess who might fall in love with Marcius and use her supernatural influence ('charms') to deflect the enemy's blades away from him. Fortune in classical and Renaissance thought was a capricious divine power over human success and failure — if she favours you, swords miss; if she turns against you, nothing can save you.
detail: Fortune (Latin Fortuna) was imagined as a goddess, often blindfolded, who distributed luck without reason, turning her wheel to raise the low and humble the great. The prayer that Fortune should 'fall in love' with Marcius is a way of asking that the warrior's luck hold: a goddess infatuated with him would avert her usual blind indifference and actively deflect harm. 'Her great charms' are her magical powers over chance — she is also a sorceress of fate. 'Prosperity be thy page!' means 'May success serve you as a page-boy serves his master.' The irony in the play's larger arc is sharp: Fortune will eventually wheel Marcius from the height of Corioli to exile and death, the classic de casibus fall. Titus Lartius's prayer is sincere, but Fortune is proverbially faithless.

sources.name: Boethius
sources.citation: Boethius, Consolatio Philosophiae II, prose 1-2 (Fortune as a goddess turning her wheel — the canonical late-antique source for the Fortune-goddess image).

sources.name: Plutarch (North)
sources.citation: Plutarch, 'Life of Coriolanus,' in The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579) — Fortune's role in the reversals of Coriolanus's career.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 532

Boethius Consolatio II, prose 1-2 is precisely where Fortune speaks and describes turning her wheel — the citation is accurate; Plutarch/North is an appropriate source for Fortune's role in the reversals of Coriolanus's career.

The personification of Fortune as a goddess whose 'charms' are magical powers over chance is a well-attested classical and Renaissance reading; 'Prosperity be thy page' as prosperous success serving as a page-boy is correct; the note about Fortune's eventual betrayal of Marcius accurately reflects the play's arc without over-reading the immediate speech.

anchor_text: we are come off Like Romans
summary: 'Come off' means to withdraw from a battle or engagement; the phrase 'come off like Romans' means they retreated in disciplined order, neither recklessly standing nor running in panic. Cominius immediately reassures his exhausted troops that an organized retirement is no disgrace.
detail: The military sense of 'come off' — to disengage, to pull back — is common in Elizabethan and Jacobean usage. Cominius frames the retreat as a tactical maneuver rather than a defeat, consistent with Roman disciplinary ideals. Plutarch's Life of Coriolanus (North 1579) stresses the Romans' ability to preserve order under pressure as a defining virtue; this speech sets up the contrast with Marcius's own reckless, single-warrior heroics.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'come off' v. phr. (sense 1b): to withdraw from a fight or contest, to escape.

sources.name: Plutarch / North
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus, ch. 8, trans. Thomas North (1579): Roman discipline in retreat.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 542

OED s.v. 'come off' sense 1b (withdrawal from a fight) is a real entry; Plutarch Life of Coriolanus ch. 8 in North's 1579 translation does describe the Roman disciplinary context of Marcius's return from Corioli — both sources genuinely support the gloss.

The scene text confirms 'come off' as a tactical withdrawal framed as disciplined rather than disgraceful ('neither foolish in our stands / Nor cowardly in retire'), and the contrast with Marcius's individual heroics is genuine in the surrounding context.

anchor_text: appear as he were flay'd
summary: 'Flay'd' means skinned — as an animal is stripped of its hide. Cominius sees a figure so drenched in blood from head to toe that his skin appears to have been peeled away. The image makes Marcius look grotesquely raw rather than merely wounded, and immediately signals his extraordinary, inhuman valour at Corioli.
detail: The flaying image recurs in the play's body-horror vocabulary for wounds and violence. In Plutarch's Life of Coriolanus (North 1579, ch. 8), Marcius returns from his solo breakthrough into Corioli covered in wounds and blood; Shakespeare translates the written description into a visual shock for the theatre audience. The detail also echoes the classical Marsyas, flayed for his musical hubris, though here the association is with martial excess rather than punishment.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'flay' v.: to strip the skin from (a person or animal).

sources.name: Plutarch / North
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus, ch. 8, trans. Thomas North (1579): description of Marcius's blood-covered return.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 567

OED s.v. 'flay' v. (to strip the skin from) is a real, uncontroversial entry; Plutarch Life of Coriolanus ch. 8 (North 1579) genuinely describes Marcius returning blood-soaked from Corioli, supporting the contextual claim.

The core gloss ('skinned, drenched in blood') is sound, but the appended Marsyas allusion ('though here the association is with martial excess rather than punishment') is a speculative classical free-association unsupported by the scene text and not endorsed by the major Coriolanus commentators — it should be trimmed or marked scholar-depth only.

anchor_text: thunder from a tabor More than I know the sound of Marcius
summary: A 'tabor' is a small, shallow drum typically beaten with one stick while the player blows a pipe with the other hand — a common instrument of street entertainers and festive processions. Cominius says he knows Marcius's voice as surely as a shepherd knows the difference between a thunderclap and a toy drum's tap: there is no possibility of confusion.
detail: The tabor-and-pipe was a one-person folk instrument associated with popular entertainment and morris dancing, not with military ceremony (where large kettledrums and trumpets were used). Placing the sheep-pasture shepherd alongside the battlefield drum contrasts the pastoral world with the military world, and the trivial tap of a tabor against the vast thunder underlines how unmistakably Marcius's voice stands out from the ordinary soldiers around him.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'tabor' n.1: a small drum, beaten with one stick, used especially to accompany a pipe.

sources.name: Onions
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary (rev. R. D. Eagleson, 1986), s.v. 'tabor': small one-headed drum.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 571

OED s.v. 'tabor' n.1 (small one-headed drum beaten with one stick, accompanying a pipe) is a standard entry, and Onions s.v. 'tabor' is a real Shakespeare Glossary entry — both sources accurately support the definition given.

The simile is read accurately: Cominius says he knows Marcius's voice as surely as a shepherd distinguishes thunder from a tabor-tap, and the gloss correctly identifies the tabor as a light folk instrument contrasted with thunder — the comparison of trivial vs. unmistakable is sound and the text supports it.

anchor_text: let me clip ye In arms as sound as when I woo'd
summary: 'Clip' means to embrace, to clasp with the arms. Marcius greets Cominius as warmly as he once courted his wife Virgilia — and 'tapers burn'd to bedward' are the wedding-night candles burning down as the bridal couple went to bed. Even in this affectionate moment, Marcius's only vocabulary for love is the language of physical strength: arms, not hands.
detail: The comparison of battlefield comradeship to the intimacy of a wedding night is characteristic of how Coriolanus relates to men who are his equals in war — his deepest emotional bonds are with Cominius and, paradoxically, with his enemy Aufidius. 'Bedward' is an adverbial compound: toward bed. 'Tapers burn'd to bedward' implies the candles were nearly burned out, i.e. the night was far spent with the newlyweds. The same earthy directness marks Volumnia's martial-mother speeches in 1.3.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'clip' v.2, sense 1: to embrace, clasp; also OED s.v. 'bedward' adv.: toward bed.

sources.name: Schmidt
sources.citation: Schmidt, A. Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874), s.v. 'clip': to hug, to embrace tightly.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 577

OED s.v. 'clip' v.2 sense 1 (to embrace) and s.v. 'bedward' adv. are real entries; Schmidt s.v. 'clip' (to hug, embrace tightly) is a genuine Shakespeare-Lexicon entry — all three senses are accurately cited.

The archaic sense of 'clip' as embrace is well-attested, and 'tapers burn'd to bedward' as wedding-night candles nearly burned out is a defensible reading supported by the text; the observation about Marcius's deepest bonds being with male military equals is a mainstream critical reading for this play.

anchor_text: The common file,--a plague!--tribunes for them!
summary: 'The common file' means the ordinary rank-and-file soldiers, not the officers. Marcius is furious that his men fled from enemy soldiers he regards as their inferiors — and his angry 'tribunes for them!' is a bitter curse: let the cowards have their tribunes (the new popular magistrates), since they're fit for nothing better than plebeian politics. The line packs Marcius's class contempt and political rage into three words.
detail: In Roman armies the 'file' was the basic tactical unit of infantry standing one behind another in formation. 'Common file' thus means the rank-and-file legionaries as opposed to centurions and officers. The tribunes of the people were newly created magistrates (494 BCE, per Livy and Plutarch) elected to protect plebeian interests — exactly the kind of institution Coriolanus regards as a cancer in the body politic. The throwaway curse foreshadows the political conflict that will destroy him: the tribunes will engineer his banishment in Acts 2-3. Plutarch (Life of Coriolanus, ch. 15) records Coriolanus's open contempt for the tribunate as the trigger for his downfall.

sources.name: Plutarch / North
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus, ch. 15, trans. Thomas North (1579): Coriolanus's contempt for the tribunes and his invective against the power they hold.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'file' n.3, sense 5: a line of soldiers standing one behind another; 'rank and file' = ordinary soldiers.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 594

OED s.v. 'file' n.3 sense 5 is credible; Plutarch ch. 15 (North 1579) is cited for Coriolanus's contempt for the tribunes as his downfall trigger, but the Greek critical text (Thayer) places this episode at section 18, not 8 or 15 — North's chapter numbering may differ, but the chapter number cannot be verified with confidence.

The military sense of 'common file' as rank-and-file infantry is accurate, and 'tribunes for them!' read as a contemptuous curse ('let them have their plebeian magistrates') is consistent with Marcius's characterisation throughout; the foreshadowing point about the tribunate engineering his banishment is defensible thematic context.

anchor_text: bands in the vaward are the Antiates, Of their best trust; o'er them Aufidius
summary: The 'vaward' is the vanguard — the forward-most division of an army and the most dangerous post. The 'Antiates' are the soldiers from Antium, the Volscians' chief city, and thus their most trusted, elite troops. Aufidius, the Volscian general, commands them personally. Marcius demands to be sent precisely against this strongest point.
detail: 'Vaward' is a contraction of 'vanguard,' itself from Old French avant-garde. In Renaissance military formation the van was where the hardest fighting happened and where the most reliable troops were placed. Antium (modern Anzio on the Italian coast, about 50 km south of Rome) was the principal city of the Volscians; Plutarch (Life of Coriolanus, ch. 23) specifies it as Aufidius's home and the Volscian political centre. Marcius seeks out Aufidius specifically because their personal rivalry — they have fought and Aufidius has always lost — is the emotional engine driving him. His request is strategically suicidal and psychologically inevitable.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'vaward' n.: the foremost division of an army; the vanguard. Also OED s.v. 'Antiate' a. and n.: of or belonging to Antium.

sources.name: Plutarch / North
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus, ch. 23, trans. Thomas North (1579): Antium as the Volscians' principal city and Aufidius's home.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 607

OED s.v. 'vaward' n. and 'Antiate' are real entries; Plutarch ch. 23 (North 1579) for Marcius's journey to Antium and Aufidius's residence there corresponds to sections 22-23 of the Greek text, plausibly ch. 23 in North's numbering — the core claims are supportable.

The military gloss on 'vaward' (vanguard) and 'Antiates' (troops from Antium) is accurate, the etymology of vanguard from avant-garde is correct, and the characterisation of Marcius's demand as 'strategically suicidal and psychologically inevitable' is a mainstream reading of his rivalry-obsession with Aufidius.

anchor_text: love this painting Wherein you see me smear'd
summary: Marcius calls his blood-drenched appearance a 'painting' — a darkly ironic metaphor for the gore covering him. Recruiting volunteers to follow him, he invites men who 'love this painting' (i.e., welcome the sight of war-blood) rather than fear it. The word choice turns his horror-show appearance into an aesthetic object, daring men to admire rather than recoil from it.
detail: The figure turns Marcius's horror-show appearance into an aesthetic object, daring men to admire rather than recoil from it. Blood-as-paint is also a visual cue for the Jacobean stage: Marcius would have been using theatrical blood (pig's blood or a red cosmetic) to achieve the shocking entrance. The metaphor carries a recruitment logic -- only those whose taste runs to such 'painting' (who find martial gore stirring rather than terrible) are fit to follow him.

anchor_text: O, me alone! Make you a sword of me?
summary: The soldiers carry Marcius on their shoulders and throw their caps in the air in acclamation. His startled response — 'Make you a sword of me?' — is a rapid metaphor: are they using him as a weapon, a mere instrument of their battle? The question is genuinely ambivalent: he is simultaneously pleased to be their champion and resistant to being an instrument of anyone else's purpose.
detail: Lifting a victorious soldier on his comrades' shoulders and tossing caps was a recognizable gesture of acclamation in Shakespeare's theatre — the stage direction 'They all shout and wave their swords; take him up in their arms and cast up their caps' is unusually explicit. The sword-metaphor also previews a central tension in the play: Rome will attempt to make Marcius into a political instrument (the consulship campaign), and his refusal to be wielded by others — tribunes, patricians, or Volumnia — drives the tragedy. 'O, me alone!' is an exclamation of shock, not pride, though its literal meaning ('only me!') equally expresses his belief that he could fight them all by himself.

anchor_text: Make good this ostentation
summary: 'Ostentation' here means display or show — not the modern sense of showy self-promotion. Cominius is telling the troops who volunteered to 'make good' (prove in action) the willingness they just demonstrated by waving their swords and cheering. The word has no negative connotation in this usage.
detail: In early modern English 'ostentation' frequently meant simply a showing, a demonstration, or a public display, without the pejorative charge it carries today. The OED records the neutral sense throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries: a public show or exhibition of something. Cominius is not accusing the soldiers of vanity; he is commending the demonstration they made and asking them to back it up in the coming fight. The line closes the scene on a note of military solidarity just before the march to engage Aufidius.

anchor_text: let the ports be guarded
summary: 'Ports' here means gates — specifically the city gates of Corioli. Lartius is ordering the garrison to keep the captured city's entrances locked and watched.

anchor_text: the rest will serve / For a short holding
summary: 'Holding' means a defensive hold — keeping possession of a place against attack for a limited time. Lartius is saying the remaining troops in the garrison are enough for a brief defense of Corioli, but if the Romans lose the battle in the field they will be unable to hold the city either.

anchor_text: Not Afric owns a serpent I abhor
summary: 'Afric' is an archaic shortened form of 'Africa,' which in classical and Renaissance writing was famed above all continents for its lethal serpents. 'Envy' here means intense hatred or ill-will, not jealousy. Aufidius is saying: not even Africa's worst snake disgusts me as much as your reputation ('fame') and your enmity toward me.
detail: The Africa-serpents topos runs from Pliny (Natural History 8-9) through Lucan's Pharsalia (Book 9, where the Libyan desert crawls with vipers and asps after the Gorgon's blood falls) to Elizabethan commonplace — Africa's 'envenomed' fauna made it a ready hyperbole for the most extreme possible hatred. Shakespeare exploits the same image in Othello (3.3, 'Pontick sea') and Antony and Cleopatra (the asp). 'Envy' in its older sense of 'malice' or 'hostility' is distinct from the modern sense of coveting another's advantage; Aufidius means the personal enmity Marcius bears him, not admiration. The compressed line packs three terms of escalation: the deadliest creature, the most infamous region, and the most visceral loathing.

anchor_text: the first budger die the other's slave
summary: 'Budger' is a rare word meaning one who budges — who flinches, yields ground, or retreats. Marcius is proposing a lethal wager: whichever of them moves backward first shall die as the other's slave. The taunt turns battlefield retreat into the worst possible humiliation for a Roman soldier.

The compound shame here — death plus slavery — reflects the Roman warrior code in which to yield was a double disgrace: it forfeited life by proving you unworthy of living freely. Plutarch's Life of Coriolanus (North 1579) emphasises Marcius's contempt for any man who hesitated in battle; the dare is entirely in character. The gods' doom mentioned in the next line ('And the gods doom him after!') adds a third sanction beyond death and slavery.

'Budger' as one who flinches or yields ground is accurate, and the double-shame construction (death plus slavery) is a defensible reading of Marcius's warrior code as established in Plutarch and the play.

anchor_text: Wert thou the Hector That was the whip of your bragg'd progeny
summary: Hector was the greatest warrior of Troy — the champion who drove back the Greeks for nine years before Achilles killed him. 'Your bragg'd progeny' means the Romans, who claimed descent from the Trojan prince Aeneas: Aufidius taunts Marcius that even the scourge of his own ancestors would not be safe from him. The insult says: your proudest myth cannot save you.
detail: Rome's legendary Trojan lineage ran from Aeneas (son of Anchises and Venus, Hector's kinsman) through his son Ascanius to Romulus and Remus, then to the city itself. Shakespeare draws on Virgil's Aeneid and North's Plutarch, both of which take the Trojan-Roman descent as established fact. Hector ('the whip') in Homer's Iliad is the Trojans' defender who slaughters Greek heroes and drives them back to their ships (Iliad 8, 11-15), but from the Romans' own genealogical perspective he is the warrior who scourged their Trojan forebears — hence 'whip of your bragg'd progeny.' Aufidius's point is precise: he is willing to face even the figure Rome boasts as its ancestral enemy; the heroic benchmark is chosen to maximize the insult. The word 'bragg'd' ('much-boasted') deflates Roman ancestral pride in the same breath that Aufidius invokes it.

sources.name: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus (North 1579)
sources.citation: Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus, in North's translation (1579); the Trojan-Roman genealogy is the background of every Roman play in the Plutarchan tradition.

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 6.369-502 (Hector) and 22.136-404 (Achilles kills Hector).
