The core reading is sound: Aufidius invokes Hector as the supreme warrior of Rome's boasted Trojan ancestry to maximize the insult — even your race's greatest hero would not save you; the annotation's phrasing about Hector 'scourging his own ancestors' is slightly confused in one sentence but does not undermine the defensible main interpretation that 'whip of your bragg'd progeny' means Hector as the paramount warrior-figure of Rome's Trojan lineage.

anchor_text: Officious, and not valiant,--you have sham'd me In your condemned seconds
summary: 'Seconds' are fighters who step in to help one side in a single combat. 'Officious' here means meddlesomely intrusive — acting out of turn — not the modern sense of over-bureaucratic. 'Condemned' means contemptible or damnable. Aufidius is furious at his own soldiers for intervening: their uninvited help is no valour but an insult, because it implies he could not beat Marcius alone.
detail: In the formal code of single combat, a 'second' was a designated assistant who might advise or, in extremity, take up the fight — but joining in without invitation was a breach of honour. Aufidius's complaint to his Volscian soldiers is the mirror of his boast that he will fight Marcius without help: the unsolicited rescue shames him because it implies he was losing, and it denies him the personal victory over his great rival that drives him throughout the play. The word 'officious' in its Elizabethan sense of 'doing more than asked, meddlesome' (OED s.v. 'officious' 2) is still in use in phrases like 'officious bystander' in English law.

anchor_text: Here is the steed, we the caparison
summary: Lartius uses a pointed metaphor: the warhorse (Marcius) is everything; the rest of the army is merely the caparison — the ornamental harness and cloth draped over the horse. The image gives Marcius all the life, force, and direction, and reduces the other soldiers to decorative equipment.
detail: A caparison is the embroidered cloth or armored covering fitted over a horse for battle or ceremony — showy but passive, deriving all meaning from the horse beneath it. The metaphor compresses Lartius's whole estimate of what happened at Corioli: Marcius acted; the army dressed the action. Shakespeare takes Plutarch's Life of Coriolanus (North, 1579) as his source throughout; Plutarch records the Senate and commanders crediting Marcius alone with the taking of the city.

anchor_text: You shall not be / The grave of your deserving
summary: Cominius tells Marcius he will not be allowed to bury his own merit — to let his great deeds go unknown and unrecorded. 'Grave' is used as a verb meaning 'burial place that silences,' not a pit in the ground.
detail: The figure treats merit as something that can be interred and forgotten. Cominius insists that Rome must be told what Marcius did, partly as a matter of justice and partly because a city that does not know the value of its own soldiers cannot protect itself. The passage echoes Plutarch's account that after Corioli the army and commanders formally praised Marcius before the assembled troops — a recognised Roman practice of public testimony to a soldier's deeds.

anchor_text: fester 'gainst ingratitude, / And tent themselves with death
summary: 'Tent' here is a surgical term: a small roll of lint or cloth pushed into a wound to keep it open and allow it to drain and heal. Cominius says that if the wounds are not acknowledged, they will fester rather than heal — probing themselves, as it were, with death instead of medicine. It is a grim image of wounds growing lethal through neglect.
detail: In early modern surgery a 'tent' (from French tente, related to 'probe') was inserted into a wound to prevent it closing on a still-infected interior; the doctor would 'tent' a wound to clean it. Cominius's conceit runs: Marcius's wounds deserve to be remembered and honored; if ingratitude silences them, they will not submit to healing but will instead probe themselves with the only instrument left — death. The image anticipates the play's broader concern with the body as an arena of honor, shame, and violence.

anchor_text: We render you the tenth; to be ta'en forth / Before the common distribution at / Your only choice
summary: Cominius offers Marcius a tenth of all the captured horses and treasure — chosen before the rest is divided among the army — as a personal reward for his valor at Corioli. This was a recognised Roman military custom: the general could set aside a prize share for an outstanding soldier before the spoils were distributed to the common soldiers.
detail: Plutarch's Life of Coriolanus records this offer: Cominius granted Marcius a tenth part of all the horses, treasure, and prisoners before the common lot was drawn, plus the special present of a richly trapped warhorse. Reserving a portion of spoils for conspicuous valour was a recognised feature of Roman military reward. Marcius's rejection of the offer -- accepting only the horse and the honour -- establishes the central paradox of his character: he courts honour but refuses its material rewards, finding them beneath his ideal of service.

anchor_text: May these same instruments which you profane / Never sound more! When drums and trumpets shall / I' the field prove flatterers, let courts and cities be / Made all of false-fac'd soothing
summary: Marcius curses the drums and trumpets his soldiers are beating to acclaim him, declaring they profane (desecrate) their proper use by turning battlefield instruments into tools of flattery. He is constructing an argument by analogy: if war's honest instruments become flatterers, then all of society — courts and cities — might as well be built of lies. 'Soothing' means empty, agreeable flattery.
detail: The rhetorical device is a formal conditional curse: 'if X, then let Y follow.' Marcius makes battlefield music the standard of truth — drums and trumpets on a field of war cannot lie, since they signal real things (advance, retreat, victory). To use them for idle cheering is to corrupt a truth-telling instrument. His disgust at applause runs through the whole play and will prove his political undoing: he cannot perform the self-display the consulship demands. 'Profane' carries its full Latin sense of treating the sacred as common.

The word survives into modern English as 'debilitate.'

anchor_text: shout me forth in acclamations hyperbolical; / As if I loved my little should be dieted / In praises sauc'd with lies
summary: The syntax is compressed and requires unpacking: 'my little' means 'my modest achievement'; 'dieted in praises sauc'd with lies' means fed (dieted) on exaggerated praise seasoned with falsehood — as food is sauced to disguise its plainness. Marcius is saying: as if I wanted my small deeds to be inflated and served up to me smothered in lies. 'Hyperbolical' is used as a straightforward adjective meaning extravagant, excessive.
detail: The food metaphor ('dieted,' 'sauc'd') is pointed: saucing was how cooks disguised plain or poor food to make it palatable. Marcius extends the metaphor to praise that dresses up nothing — his modest deeds — as though they were a great feast. The word 'hyperbolical' (from Greek hyperbole, 'excess') would have been recognisable to educated audience members as a rhetorical term for deliberate exaggeration, and Marcius is accusing the soldiers of using exactly that figure. The inverted syntax ('my little should be dieted') puts the object before the verb, which is common in Shakespeare but can confuse modern readers.

anchor_text: For what he did before Corioli, call him, / With all the applause--and clamour of the host, / 'Caius Marcius Coriolanus.'
summary: Cominius formally confers the surname 'Coriolanus' on Caius Marcius before the assembled army. This was an actual Roman practice: a general or the Senate could award an honorific surname (called an agnomen) derived from the place of a great victory. 'Coriolanus' means, simply, 'the man who took Corioli.'
detail: Plutarch records this award exactly: Cominius, on behalf of the people and Senate, gave Marcius the name Coriolanus for his single-handed breach of the gates of Corioli. Historical Roman examples of such victory-surnames include Africanus (Scipio, conqueror of Carthage), Macedonicus, and Asiaticus. The surname marks the hinge of the play's first act and of the hero's identity: for the rest of the play he is 'Coriolanus,' a name that embeds his greatest achievement and, ultimately, the source of the grievance that destroys him — he took the city of the people who will eventually kill him.

anchor_text: To undercrest your good addition / To the fairness of my power
summary: 'Addition' means a title added to a person's name — here, the surname 'Coriolanus.' 'Undercrest' is a heraldic term: a crest is the badge of arms worn on top of a helmet; to 'undercrest' an addition is to support it, to be the worthy bearer who lives up to what the title claims. A 'crest' was the device on top of a helmet that identified the knight in battle and tournament, and 'to bear' a crest was to live up to the honor it signified. Here Marcius recoins the verb: he will 'under-crest' (stand beneath and support) Cominius's 'addition' (the new name) to the best of his ability. The phrasing accepts the honor conditionally — he will try to deserve it — which reads as humility but also as a refusal to be fully satisfied by external titles. 'To the fairness of my power' = 'as honestly as I am able.'

anchor_text: mine emulation / Hath not that honour in't it had
summary: 'Emulation' in Elizabethan usage means jealous, competitive rivalry — not the modern sense of imitation or admiration. anchor_text: I'll potch at him some way, / Or wrath or craft may get him
summary: 'Potch' means to jab or thrust, as with a weapon — here Aufidius says he will attack Marcius by any dirty means, either in a rage ('wrath') or by trickery ('craft'), since honorable equal combat has never worked. Its roughness is deliberate: after the lofty claim of 'true sword to sword,' Aufidius drops to a curt, blunt word for underhanded stabbing. anchor_text: nor sleep nor sanctuary, / Being naked, sick; nor fane nor Capitol
summary: Aufidius swears that no Roman protection will shield Marcius: not 'sanctuary' (the custom that a temple or altar made a fugitive inviolable), not a 'fane' (an archaic word for a temple or shrine), not even the Capitol, Rome's most sacred citadel. He is renouncing every ancient convention that put holy spaces and the helpless beyond a warrior's reach.

'Naked' and 'sick' specify the most pitiable condition a suppliant could be in. Aufidius goes through the whole list systematically -- sleep, sanctuary, temple, the Capitol, priestly prayers, times of sacrifice -- to insist his hatred overrides every civilizing constraint. 'Fane' is from Latin fanum, a consecrated place; it was already archaic in Shakespeare's day, chosen here for its specifically Roman flavour. The catalogue of violated sanctities is Shakespeare's own dramatic elaboration of Plutarch's portrait of Aufidius's implacable enmity.

anchor_text: upon my brother's guard, even there, / Against the hospitable canon, would I / Wash my fierce hand in's heart
summary: The 'hospitable canon' is the ancient law of hospitality: a host is obliged to protect any guest under his roof, and killing a guest-friend is a grave religious and social transgression. Aufidius says that even if Marcius were a guest in his own house, sheltered by his brother's personal guarantee, he would still murder him — deliberately breaking the most sacred bond of peaceful society.
detail: The Greek concept of xenia (guest-friendship) and its Roman equivalent had near-sacred force in antiquity: violating it was an offense against the gods as well as against social order. Aufidius names his own 'brother's guard' — i.e., his brother acting as personal pledge for the guest's safety — to make clear he would betray even his own kin's word. The image of 'washing' his hand in Marcius's heart is a deliberately shocking reversal of the normal ritual hand-washing of host and guest. Shakespeare returns to this violation of hospitality: when the exiled Coriolanus actually does go to Aufidius's house in Act 4, Aufidius (remarkably) honors the guest-law at that moment — which makes his later betrayal all the more pointed in retrospect. Plutarch's North records no such explicit vow, making this passage Shakespeare's dramatic intensification of the rivalry.

The College of Augurs oversaw the reading of birds, thunder, and other signs; their reports were taken seriously in public life. Here the augurer's reading of signs about Coriolanus's return sets an atmosphere of official, supernatural anticipation around the news of the battle.

anchor_text: of us o' the right-hand file
summary: 'The right-hand file' means the patricians, the noble class — Menenius places himself and his social equals in this category as opposed to the tribunes and the common people. 'File' is a military term for a column of soldiers; the right of the line was the position of honor in a Roman army.
detail: The Roman army drew up with the most experienced troops on the right wing (the position farthest from the protection of one's own shield). Menenius adapts the military image to social rank: he belongs to the patrician 'right-hand file,' the faction of men like himself and Coriolanus. The phrase ironically undercuts the tribunes' claim to speak for Rome, since in this formulation they are not even in the honorable column.

anchor_text: turn your eyes toward the napes of your necks, and make but an interior survey
summary: Menenius uses a grotesque impossible-image to say the tribunes should examine their own faults before accusing Coriolanus of pride. If they could twist their eyes to look at the backs of their own heads, they would see what hypocrites they are — a comic physical image for self-examination.

It is Menenius's satirical variation on the classical advice 'Know thyself' (the Delphic maxim). The speech builds toward his catalog of the tribunes' public misbehavior, making the self-examination argument a setup for his attack.

anchor_text: a humorous patrician
summary: 'Humorous' here means full of mood-swings or whims, unpredictably temperamental — not funny. In Elizabethan medicine the four 'humors' (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) governed personality; an excess of any one made a person erratic. Menenius cheerfully concedes that he is known for his changeable temper.

'Humorous' in Shakespeare usually means governed by unpredictable impulse, as in Menenius's self-portrait here — quick to anger, quick to laugh.

anchor_text: not a drop of allaying Tiber in't
summary: 'Allaying' means diluting or weakening. It was common in Shakespeare's time to water down wine; Menenius jokes that he drinks his wine undiluted — strong and unadulterated — unlike the tepid, compromising posture he ascribes to the tribunes. The Tiber is the river running through Rome.

anchor_text: converses more with the buttock of the night than with the forehead of the morning

anchor_text: the ass in compound with the major part of your syllables
summary: Menenius embeds an insult in pedantic language: 'the ass in compound' with their syllables means that the word 'ass' (fool/donkey) is hidden inside their speech — their official words contain 'ass.' The Latinate word 'compound' (mixed together) makes the pun scholarly in style while crude in content.

anchor_text: orange-wife and a fosset-seller, and then rejourn the controversy of threepence
summary: Menenius mocks the tribunes' actual work as magistrates: they spend the morning judging petty disputes — an orange-seller (a woman who sells oranges, the cheapest fruit) against a faucet-seller (a vendor of tap-fittings and spigots). anchor_text: set up the bloody flag against all patience
summary: A red or 'bloody' flag (a 'vexillum') was the ancient Roman signal for war — when the red flag was raised above the general's tent, the army prepared to fight. Menenius's point is darkly comic: the tribunes cannot even get through a court hearing without their physical weakness disrupting the proceedings. The military image applied to a bout of colic cuts the tribunes down to size — they are at war only with their own bowels.

anchor_text: worth all your predecessors since Deucalion
summary: Deucalion was the Greek Noah — the survivor of the great flood who repopulated the world. detail: In Greek myth Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha were the sole survivors when Zeus flooded the earth to destroy a corrupt humanity; they repopulated it by throwing stones (the bones of their mother, Earth) over their shoulders, which became new people. The hyperbole also quietly ridicules the tribunes' ancestry, since Menenius adds that 'some of the best of 'em were hereditary hangmen.'

The public proclamation by a herald makes the naming official and civic, turning individual valor into a civic identity.

anchor_text: My gracious silence, hail
summary: Coriolanus greets his weeping wife Virgilia as 'My gracious silence' — a term of endearment that also perfectly describes her character. Where Volumnia speaks boldly and argues loudly, Virgilia is almost always quiet; her silence is not weakness but a profound, eloquent restraint. It is one of the play's most famous and tender lines.
detail: The oxymoronic quality of 'gracious silence' — silence being nothing, yet here named and praised — is a form of apostrophe (addressing an abstraction or quality as if it were a person). 'Gracious' carries both its modern sense of gentle kindness and its older sense of grace, of divine favor. The line defines Virgilia in a single phrase: she weeps rather than speaks, and in that weeping she is everything Coriolanus's mother is not. The contrast with Volumnia's forthright, argumentative character is immediately present on stage.

'Reechy' derives from 'reek' (smoke, stench); it describes both the neck and the kitchen environment. The social comedy underlines how total the enthusiasm for Coriolanus is — even those with no stake in politics want to see the hero.

anchor_text: seld-shown flamens do press among the popular throngs
summary: A flamen (plural flamines) was a Roman priest assigned to the cult of a specific god — usually kept to temple duties and subject to strict rules that prevented them from mixing freely in public. anchor_text: The napless vesture of humility
summary: The 'gown (vesture) of humility' was the plain white toga a consul-candidate was required to wear when canvassing the Roman people for their votes. 'Napless' means worn smooth, without any nap (the raised surface of cloth) — threadbare. Brutus reports that Coriolanus has sworn he would never put on this deliberately humble garment to beg the citizens' suffrages.

'Napless' intensifies the humiliation — the gown is not just plain but worn bare, the most deliberately impoverished garment. Coriolanus's refusal to wear it is the pivot of the play's political crisis: the tribunes know he cannot bear this ritual, and they plan to exploit his inability to perform it.

anchor_text: his sword,--death's stamp,-- / Where it did mark, it took
summary: Cominius compares Coriolanus's sword to a die or seal ('death's stamp') that, wherever it strikes an impression, completes the transaction — kills. anchor_text: Put on the gown, stand naked, and entreat them

Coriolanus's disgust at this custom — showing scars for 'hire' of the people's breath — is the scene's central conflict. anchor_text: You see how he intends to use the people

Sicinius's line 'May they perceive's intent!' is ambiguous: it could mean 'I hope the people see through him' or 'let his contempt be obvious so we can exploit it.' summary: The Third Citizen's speech is built on a paradox: the citizens have the legal power to withhold their votes, yet feel morally obliged to grant them. The metaphor of illegitimate speech reframes lying as a lesser, forgivable sin, distinct from his 'real' self — an argument designed to allow him to flatter without feeling that he has compromised his identity.
detail: The word 'bastard' carried a strong legal and social charge: a child born outside wedlock had no legal right to inheritance or recognition. Volumnia extends this to language: the flattering words he will say are disowned by his true self and carry no moral weight. The argument is ethically slippery — it invites him to develop a split between performed and real identity, which the play's theatrical metaphors throughout this scene reinforce. 'Allowance' = authorization, approval (Schmidt, s.v.).

anchor_text: Action is eloquence, and the eyes of the ignorant More learned than the ears
summary: Volumnia invokes the classical principle that physical gesture communicates more persuasively to an uneducated crowd than spoken argument. She is drawing on the rhetoric tradition: Cicero and Quintilian both ranked 'actio' (bodily delivery) as one of the five parts of oratory and sometimes called it the most powerful. The irony is that she is coaching Rome's greatest soldier in stagecraft — the one art he despises.

anchor_text: show them my unbarb'd sconce
summary: 'Unbarb'd' means without armour — literally without the protective barb or covering. 'Sconce' is slang for head. Coriolanus is bitterly asking whether he must show the plebeians his bare, unprotected, unhelmeted head — a gesture of submission and vulnerability that he finds as degrading as appearing naked before an enemy.

anchor_text: possess me Some harlot's spirit! My throat of war be turn'd, Which quired with my drum, into a pipe Small as an eunuch
summary: In a sustained self-curse, Coriolanus prays to be stripped of his own identity and replaced with degrading substitutes: a prostitute's dissembling soul, a war-voice shrunk to a eunuch's falsetto, a soldier's eyes flooded with schoolboys' tears, and knees trained only for the stirrup now bent like a beggar's. The speech is built as a series of grotesque transformations — a rhetorical figure called enumeratio — measuring the distance between what he is and what he is being asked to become.
detail: 'Harlot' in Shakespeare often means a male entertainer or rogue (Schmidt, s.v.) as well as a prostitute; here the sense is a performer who sells appealing pretense. 'Quired' = chorused or sang in choir: his battle-voice was once orchestrated with drums; now it must shrink. A eunuch's high voice was a musical commonplace — court choirs employed castrati specifically for their unbroken treble — and so the contrast between the drum and the pipe collapses martial manhood into feminized performance. The whole speech is a theatrically self-aware enactment of the very acting it protests: Coriolanus performs his refusal to perform.

anchor_text: I'll mountebank their loves, Cog their hearts from them
summary: 'Mountebank' as a verb means to swindle or trick, from the Italian mountebank (a quack who climbed onto a bench to hawk fake remedies at markets). 'Cog' means to cheat or wheedle — to pick their hearts out of them by fraud, the way a card-cheat cogs a die. Coriolanus now commits to the performance his mother urged, but frames it entirely as con-artistry, which signals he has not changed but only added a mask.
detail: A mountebank was a specific early modern figure: a traveling showman-healer who sold patent medicines from a raised platform, drawing crowds by theatrical patter. The word already carried a strong sense of theatrical fakery layered over commercial fraud. By choosing this word and 'cog,' Coriolanus shows he understands the coming marketplace performance as exactly what his mother's 'honour and policy' argument tried to dignify — shameless deception. The bitterness of the passage undercuts Volumnia's apparent victory: his compliance is furious, and the audience knows he cannot sustain it.

anchor_text: charge him home, that he affects Tyrannical power
summary: The tribunes plan their strategy before Coriolanus arrives: 'charge him home' means press the accusation hard and decisively, hitting the most damaging point — that Coriolanus seeks one-man 'tyrannical power.' The word 'tyrant' carried enormous weight in Rome: every Roman citizen knew the story of how Tarquin the Proud was driven out and the Republic founded, so calling a man tyrannical was a capital charge.
detail: Brutus's opening line maps the tribunes' rhetorical tactics: if the tyranny charge sticks, use his 'envy' (hostility) to the people as backup, and the undistributed spoils of the Antiates as a third count. 'Affect' means to seek or aspire to — the charge is not that he has seized power but that he desires it, which was enough under the Republic's deep allergy to monarchy. North's Plutarch records that the Coriolanus figure was accused of 'aiming at tyranny' during the grain-distribution dispute (Life of Coriolanus 15).

The gloss is accurate: 'charge him home' means press the accusation decisively, 'affect' means to aspire to, and the tyranny charge as a capital offense under the Republic is a sound, mainstream reading supported by both Plutarch and the text.

anchor_text: all the voices that we have procur'd, Set down by the poll
summary: 'Voices' are votes or suffrages — each citizen's verbal declaration of support. 'Set down by the poll' means recorded head by head (a 'poll' is literally a head), man by man rather than by tribe as a whole. Sicinius's next question — 'Have you collected them by tribes?' — shows Roman voting could be counted either way. The tribunes want a full tally both individually and by tribal division so they know their numbers exactly.
detail: Roman popular assemblies voted by tribes (the comitia tributa) — Rome was divided into thirty-five voting tribes, urban and rural — but individual voices within a tribe still mattered for canvassing. In the consulship scenes the tribunes manipulate which citizens appear for or against Coriolanus; here they check their count before the trial to be sure they have the numbers for any sentence from 'fine' to 'death' to 'banishment.' Plutarch notes that the tribunes carefully prepared the popular meeting before bringing Coriolanus before it (Life of Coriolanus 18).

anchor_text: Put him to choler straight: he hath been us'd Ever to conquer
summary: 'Choler' is the hot, angry humor — according to the Elizabethan theory of the four humors (blood, phlegm, choler, melancholy), a person's character is ruled by whichever fluid predominates in the body. An excess of choler makes a man quick to fury and impossible to restrain once inflamed. Brutus's plan is simple: provoke Coriolanus into rage, because once 'chaf'd' (heated, like a chafed animal pulling at its rein) he will lose all political self-control and condemn himself out of his own mouth.
detail: The humoral framework was standard medical and theatrical language in Shakespeare's day; Coriolanus is the play's supreme choleric character. Brutus's analysis — 'being once chaf'd, he cannot / Be rein'd again to temperance' — is exact: the entire scene proves it. The word 'rein'd' (pulled back as with a horse's rein) is the play's habitual vocabulary of animal control applied to Coriolanus; Menenius will beg him to 'go about it' calmly, and Cominius to 'know' himself. The tribunes are exploiting a character flaw both sides acknowledge openly.

anchor_text: as an ostler, that for the poorest piece Will bear the knave by the volume
summary: An 'ostler' (also spelled 'hostler') was a stable-hand who looked after horses at an inn; it was a low-status, poorly paid job. Coriolanus's point — despite Menenius begging him to stay calm — is ironic: he will be calm 'as an ostler who for the smallest coin endures insult in bulk' (a man who swallows endless abuse because he must). He is ironically promising patience he does not feel; the prayer that follows is his only genuine composure before he erupts.
detail: A 'knave' is a rogue or insult; 'by the volume' means in large quantities, at length. The ostler simile is one of the play's many rank-comparisons: Coriolanus likens himself to a laborer whose endurance is merely mercenary. Within a dozen lines the ironic claim will collapse entirely when he calls the people 'curs.' 'Piece' here is a small coin — perhaps a penny or halfpenny — the pittance an ostler earned for tolerating the abuse of travelers.

anchor_text: wounds his body bears, which show Like graves i' the holy churchyard
summary: Menenius pleads Coriolanus's wounds as evidence of his service to Rome, using a striking simile: the scars lie in his flesh 'like graves in a churchyard' — grim, numerous, each one a death he nearly died. The image transforms the soldier's scarred body into a memorial landscape. The irony is immediate: Coriolanus dismisses the same wounds as 'scratches with briers' in the very next line.
detail: The 'holy churchyard' grounding the simile is a rare Christian-era intrusion in an otherwise pagan-Roman play, and it heightens the solemnity Menenius is trying to inject. Plutarch records that the tradition of the candidacy in a loose toga was specifically to let the people see the wounds (Life of Coriolanus 14); Menenius is restating that Roman argument in this new context. Coriolanus's instant deflation of the heroic simile — 'scars to move laughter only' — reveals both his contempt for the process and his genuine inability to perform the requested deference.

anchor_text: being pass'd for consul with full voice, I am so dishonour'd that the very hour You take it off again
summary: Coriolanus says he was 'passed' (approved and confirmed) as consul by 'full voice' — the people's unanimous vote — and that the tribunes are now stripping that award from him within hours of its being granted. This is his genuine grievance before the formal charges are read: the consulship was won, ratified by all parties, and then revoked by the same authority that just gave it. For him it is the deeper humiliation — not a failure to earn it, but a promise broken.
detail: In the earlier marketplace scenes (2.3) the citizens gave Coriolanus their individual voices, and the Senate confirmed him as consul; Brutus and Sicinius then persuaded the citizens to rescind their votes, leading to the confrontation in 3.1 and now this trial. The step from 'you were consul' to 'you are charged with treason' inside a single day dramatizes how fragile the consulship is when it depends on popular goodwill that the tribunes control.

anchor_text: contriv'd to take From Rome all season'd office
summary: 'Season'd office' means established, long-standing offices of government — institutions 'seasoned' (matured, tested by time, confirmed by custom) rather than new creations. Sicinius charges that Coriolanus plotted to abolish Rome's ancient constitutional offices and replace them with his own unchecked power. 'Wind / Yourself into a power tyrannical' in the next lines elaborates: he has allegedly been worming his way gradually into sole authority.
detail: 'Season'd' carries the same sense as 'seasoned timber' — hardened and proved by time. The charge that Coriolanus wanted to dismantle the republic's governing structure — Senate, consulship, tribunate — was the political form the tyranny accusation took. North's Plutarch phrases it similarly: the tribunes accused him of 'taking away the authority and power of the people' (Life of Coriolanus 18).

anchor_text: The fires i' the lowest hell fold in the people
summary: Coriolanus's outburst is a curse: 'let the fires of the deepest hell swallow the people whole.' 'Fold in' means to envelop, wrap up, engulf — as if hellfire were a great garment pulling them in. The phrase violates his promise to stay calm and proves the tribunes' strategy exactly right: the word 'traitor' has detonated him, and everything he says now seals his doom.
detail: This is the moment Brutus predicted: 'being once chaf'd, he cannot / Be rein'd again to temperance.' 'Fold in' (sometimes emended) means to close around and swallow; the image is of a vast, consuming fire enclosing and destroying. In a Roman dramatic setting 'hell' is a loose anachronism (Pluto's underworld), but Shakespeare's vocabulary reaches instinctively for Christian hell as the extreme term of damnation. The excess of the curse — damning the whole people — is exactly the evidence Sicinius needs to silence him and announce the sentence.

anchor_text: To the rock, to the rock, with him!
summary: The citizens are calling for Coriolanus to be thrown from the Tarpeian Rock — a cliff on the Capitoline Hill in Rome from which condemned traitors were hurled to their deaths. This was the ultimate Roman state execution for enemies of the people. The shout shows the crowd's first, most extreme impulse; the tribunes then pull back to the lesser sentence of banishment, which they have actually staged.
detail: The Tarpeian Rock (Rupes Tarpeia) was a steep face of the Capitoline Hill; tradition held it was named for Tarpeia, who allegedly betrayed Rome to the Sabines. The standard punishment for convicted traitors under the Republic was to be cast from this cliff. Coriolanus himself defiantly invites the sentence moments later: 'Let them pronounce the steep Tarpeian death' (TLN 2228). Plutarch records that during the confrontation with the tribunes the people clamoured that Marcius be thrown from the Tarpeian Rock.

anchor_text: pronounce the steep Tarpeian death, Vagabond exile, flaying, pent to linger
summary: Coriolanus lists the worst punishments Rome can inflict — death from the Tarpeian Rock, rootless exile, 'flaying' (being skinned alive), and being imprisoned with just enough food to stay barely alive ('pent to linger / But with a grain a day') — and says he would not give a single polite word to buy off any of them. The defiant catalog is meant to show that he is incapable of the submission being demanded of him.
detail: 'Vagabond exile' strips a Roman of citizenship, legal protection, and every civic tie — to be declared an 'enemy' and expelled was one of the severest political sentences. 'Flaying' and prison-on-starvation-rations were forms of torture and slow execution. Coriolanus invokes them all not to beg mercy but to prove he cares nothing for mercy: 'I would not buy / Their mercy at the price of one fair word.' This is the same pride that doomed him in the candidacy scenes — he cannot perform deference even to save his own life.

anchor_text: banish him our city, In peril of precipitation From off the rock Tarpeian
summary: Sicinius pronounces the formal sentence of banishment: Coriolanus must leave Rome forever, with the Tarpeian Rock as the penalty for returning. 'Precipitation' means being thrown headlong from a height — the technical term for the Tarpeian execution. The sentence is legally imposed 'in the name o' the people' and 'in the power of us the tribunes,' the two constitutional authorities the tribunes wield.
detail: The sentence formula is deliberate and public, modeled on the actual form of Roman tribal-assembly verdicts, as Shakespeare found it in North's Plutarch: 'We condemn him to everlasting banishment' (Life of Coriolanus 20). 'In peril of precipitation' is the Latin legal idiom turned into English: the sentence of exile carries with it death for violation. The legal structure — sentence in the people's name, enforced by the tribunes' authority — is the constitutional form that the tribunes have been constructing all scene; the choreographed shouts of the crowd are the ratification.

anchor_text: You common cry of curs! whose breath I hate As reek o' the rotten fens
summary: Coriolanus's farewell speech opens with a cascade of contempt in three similes: the people are a 'common cry of curs' (a pack of howling dogs — 'cry' is the technical term for a pack of hounds); their breath is as foul as the stench rising from rotting marshes ('fens'); their love is worth no more than the smell of unburied corpses. Each image combines sound, smell, and decay to express Coriolanus's total rejection of the crowd.

The 'reek o' the rotten fens' reaches for the worst smell he can summon — marshland rot releasing vaporous miasma, which Elizabethans associated with disease and poison. 'Dead carcasses of unburied men' is the extreme: without burial, a body was neither honored nor disposed of in either Roman or Christian terms. The three-part anaphoric structure ('whose breath... whose loves... that do') is itself a rhetorical device — accumulation (or auxesis) loading contempt upon contempt before the climactic reversal 'I banish you.'

anchor_text: I banish you; And here remain with your uncertainty
summary: Coriolanus reverses the sentence that has just been pronounced on him: instead of accepting banishment, he declares that he banishes Rome. The rhetorical pivot — using the very word 'banish' that was just applied to him, and turning it back on the thousands assembled — transforms humiliation into contempt. What follows is a prophecy of Rome's defenseless future without him, structured as a series of imperatives and predictions.
detail: The reversal is both theatrical and psychologically precise: Coriolanus cannot accept any verdict that places the people above him, so he reframes the entire situation — the city has expelled its only defender, not the tribune-process its enemy. The speech predicts that Rome's 'enemies, with nodding of their plumes, / Fan you into despair' — a military forecast that the play will immediately begin to fulfill as Coriolanus joins the Volscians. 'There is a world elsewhere' (TLN 2279) is the exit line: defiance in four words, a refusal to regard Rome as the measure of all things. North's Plutarch records that Coriolanus left Rome 'in a great rage and fury' (Life of Coriolanus 20).

The rhetorical reversal — Coriolanus turning the word 'banish' back on Rome — is the scene's defining theatrical gesture and is correctly described; 'There is a world elsewhere' as a defiant refusal to regard Rome as the measure of all things is a mainstream and textually grounded reading.

anchor_text: beast With many heads butts me away
summary: The crowd is imagined as a single monstrous animal with many heads — a Roman and Renaissance image for an unruly mob that acts without reason. Coriolanus has just been driven into exile by popular vote, and here he reduces the Roman citizens to a mindless brute that has battered him aside.

Shakespeare uses the image throughout the play: the tribunes call the people 'the many-headed multitude' (2.3), and Coriolanus himself elsewhere calls them 'the beast / With many heads.' The Hydra, the nine-headed serpent of myth, supplied one version; political theorists from Plato to Machiavelli warned against the 'multitude' as a monster. In Plutarch's Life of Coriolanus, Marcius's contempt for the common people is the root cause of his downfall, and his departure from Rome is the direct consequence of their vote for his banishment.

anchor_text: seem humbler after it is done Than when it was a-doing

The tribunes' political shrewdness is consistently contrasted with their cowardice in this same scene, where they immediately want to flee Volumnia.

anchor_text: Anger's my meat; I sup upon myself, And so shall starve with feeding
summary: Volumnia refuses Menenius's invitation to supper with a paradox: her anger feeds on herself, so the more she 'eats' it the more she wastes away. The image captures self-consuming grief — emotion that sustains you and destroys you at the same time.

Volumnia's anger is the only thing keeping her alive after the banishment of her son, but it is also eating her from within. The line is among the most compressed and memorable in the play — a couplet that does the work of a whole soliloquy on grief and fury.

anchor_text: In anger, Juno-like

Volumnia's self-identification with Juno is precisely calibrated: she does not claim divine power but divine bearing, the composure that turns grief into grandeur rather than 'faint puling.' The allusion also foreshadows the great embassy scene (5.3), where Volumnia will need exactly this iron self-command to make Coriolanus yield.

anchor_text: dissension of a doit, break out
summary: A 'doit' was the smallest Dutch or Scottish coin in circulation, worth a tiny fraction of a penny — a byword for something utterly worthless. 'Dissension of a doit' means a quarrel over nothing, a falling-out over the most trivial of pretexts. Coriolanus is saying that friends who seem inseparable can be split apart by a cause too small to name.
detail: The doit appears several times in Shakespeare as the emblem of the negligible (OED s.v. 'doit': 'a small Dutch copper coin ... used proverbially for any trifle'; also Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'doit'). The observation is also self-implicating: Coriolanus's own banishment grew from a political quarrel whose immediate trigger (his refusal to show his wounds to the plebeians) might seem equally petty to an outsider.

anchor_text: interjoin their issues
summary: 'Interjoin their issues' means to interweave their fates, concerns, and even bloodlines — to become bound together in a way that makes separation impossible. anchor_text: Fights dragon-like, and does achieve as soon As draw his sword
summary: The dragon in classical and Renaissance tradition was the supreme emblem of unstoppable military ferocity — a creature that breathes fire and cannot be checked by ordinary force. To fight 'dragon-like' means Coriolanus wins almost before the battle begins: his drawing his sword and his victory are simultaneous.
detail: Classical epic and myth gave the dragon a fixed place as the guardian-monster and the ultimate adversary (the Hydra, the Colchian serpent, the dragon of the Hesperides — all faced by Hercules or Jason). In Renaissance heraldry the dragon was a charge associated with supreme martial courage. Aufidius's grudging compliment encapsulates the paradox of the scene: the man eclipsing him is so formidable that even Aufidius cannot honestly diminish him. Ovid's Metamorphoses catalogues the great dragons in the context of heroic labours (e.g. Metamorphoses 7.149-158, the Colchian serpent; 9.182-200, Hercules).

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2938

Ovid Met. 7.149-158 correctly describes the Colchian dragon guarding the Golden Fleece; Met. 9.182-200 is Hercules's agonized recounting of his labours including serpents (Lernean Hydra, cradle-snakes), so the lines do reference serpents/monsters, but the passage is an anguished monologue rather than a narrative catalogue of heroic labours, making the citation technically supportable but imprecise.

Calling 'dragon-like' a classical allusion is a mild over-categorisation — the phrase invokes a conventional emblem of ferocity rather than any specific myth — but the core reading of unstoppable martial power is mainstream and the Ovid/heraldry framing is defensible if slightly over-pinned.

anchor_text: the osprey to the fish, who takes it By sovereignty of nature
summary: Elizabethans believed that the osprey (a large fish-eating hawk) exercised a kind of natural magnetic power over fish: the fish would turn belly-up in the water at the osprey's approach, surrendering without a struggle. Aufidius is saying that every city and garrison yields to Coriolanus as if compelled by nature itself — not by force alone, but by some irresistible authority.

anchor_text: Carry his honours even: whether 'twas pride
summary: To 'carry his honours even' means to bear his success without losing his balance — to handle distinction without being toppled by it. Aufidius goes on to diagnose Coriolanus's three possible fatal flaws: pride corrupting a lucky man; poor political judgment; or an inability to shift from soldier to statesman — 'from the casque to the cushion.' The casque is the iron helmet of war; the cushion is the padded seat of the Senate council-chamber. Coriolanus commands both with the same rigid, uncompromising temper, and that rigidity has destroyed him.
detail: The 'casque' (helmet) versus 'cushion' (cushioned senate chair) antithesis is Aufidius's sharpest psychological observation in the play: Coriolanus could not turn off the austerity of the battlefield once he entered the political arena. Plutarch makes the same diagnosis — that Coriolanus's virtues in war became vices in peacetime because he refused to moderate them (Life of Coriolanus, ch. 15, North 1579). The passage also introduces 'spices of them all' (traces of all three faults), where 'spices' means 'samples' or 'touches' (OED s.v. 'spice' n. 4b).

The casque (war-helmet) / cushion (senate seat) antithesis is the standard, uncontroversial reading, and the Plutarch ch. 15 parallel — wartime virtues becoming peacetime vices — is authentic and on point.

anchor_text: One fire drives out one fire; one nail, one nail
summary: Aufidius caps his analysis with two proverbs: fire can only be smothered by a counter-fire, and a nail can only be driven out by hammering in a new nail behind it. Both sayings mean that a superior force replaces an inferior one of the same kind. Aufidius means that Coriolanus replaced him in the Volscians' loyalty — and once Coriolanus takes Rome, something else will replace Coriolanus in turn, including Aufidius himself, who plans to be that 'new nail.'
detail: Both proverbial expressions were current in Elizabethan English. William Camden records 'one nail drives out another' (Remains Concerning Britain, 1605); the fire-quenching-fire image appears in Romeo and Juliet ('One fire burns out another's burning,' 1.2.46) and in Erasmus's Adages (Adagia 1.2.4, 'clavus clavo pellitur,' 'a nail by a nail,' widely cited in Renaissance Europe). The couplet rhyme and the parallel structure (anaphora: 'One... one; one... one') give the thought an aphoristic finality that functions as a preview of the play's catastrophe: by the logic he has just stated, Aufidius will be the new nail that drives out Coriolanus.

anchor_text: titleless, Till he had forg'd himself a name i' the fire
summary: Coriolanus has told Cominius that, having been stripped of his Roman name and civic identity by banishment, he now has no self until he burns Rome and so 'forges' — hammers out as a blacksmith hammers iron in fire — a new identity from the act of destruction. The word 'forg'd' puns on both metalwork and forgery: the name he makes will be at once heroically earned and a kind of counterfeit self.
detail: Plutarch's Life of Coriolanus records that after banishment Marcius declared 'he would give them to wete that he had yet a spirit and courage in him' (North 1579). Shakespeare concentrates that wounded pride into the image of self-creation through destruction: name in Rome is gone, so only the fire that consumes Rome can produce a new one. The forge-image also glances at his surname itself: 'Coriolanus' was a name coined from conquest (the stormed city Corioli), so his identity has always been manufactured in military fire. Now he threatens to repeat the process at Rome's expense.

The core gloss — banishment strips his Roman identity and 'forg'd' puns on blacksmithing and fabrication — is sound and mainstream; the observation that 'Coriolanus' was itself a name coined from conquest is textually grounded (Cominius explicitly says so in 2.2) and Plutarch-based, making the reflexive forge-image defensible rather than an over-reading.

anchor_text: pair of tribunes that have rack'd for Rome, To make coals cheap
summary: Menenius mocks the tribunes with furious sarcasm: 'rack'd' means both 'laboured hard' (done their utmost) and 'caused great suffering' (as on the torture-rack). Their magnificent achievement is making 'coals cheap' — a sardonic way of saying they have ensured Rome will burn, supplying plenty of cheap fuel. The two senses collapse together: they worked hard to ruin Rome.
detail: The coal image is also brutally economical: Rome is about to be set alight by Coriolanus, so coals will be 'cheap' in the sense that there will be no shortage of them. 'Rack' in the sense of causing suffering or destroying (cf. 'rack and ruin') reinforces the double meaning. The whole speech (TLN 2989-2991) is Menenius's bitter irony directed at the tribunes: 'you have made good work!' — a sarcastic credit for their successful campaign to banish Coriolanus, which has now brought the Volscian army to the city gates.

anchor_text: pick them in a pile Of noisome musty chaff
summary: 'Noisome' means foul-smelling and harmful — it comes from 'noy' (annoy, harm), not from 'noise,' so it is about stench rather than sound. 'Musty chaff' is the worthless, reeking husks of grain left after threshing. Coriolanus told Cominius he cannot pause to sift one or two good individuals ('grains') out of a reeking pile of worthless husks — meaning the Roman people who banished him.
detail: The grain-and-chaff image carries a bitter agricultural irony: Coriolanus, who despised the people's grain-riots in Act 1, now treats the entire citizenry as chaff fit only to burn. 'Noisome' (OED s.v. 'noisome,' from Middle English 'noysome,' harmful, noxious) is frequently misread by modern students as 'noisy.' The metaphor anticipates Menenius's self-identification at TLN 3004-3008: 'I am one of those; his mother, wife, / His child, and this brave fellow too — we are the grains: / You are the musty chaff.'

anchor_text: a discontented friend, grief-shot With his unkindness
summary: 'Grief-shot' is a compound adjective meaning 'pierced or wounded by grief,' on the model of 'thunderstruck' or 'love-shot' — as if sorrow were an arrow or bullet that had entered the body. Menenius imagines returning not as a failed negotiator but as a personally wounded friend, hurt by Coriolanus's coldness ('unkindness') rather than simply unsuccessful.

'Unkindness' in Elizabethan English carries more weight than it does in modern usage: 'kind' derived from 'kin,' so 'unkindness' means a breach of natural bond between kinfolk or close friends, not merely a small rudeness. Menenius is admitting that being turned away by someone he regards almost as a son would wound him in that deeper, familial sense.

anchor_text: He was not taken well: he had not din'd; The veins unfill'd, our blood is cold
summary: Menenius explains why Cominius's mission failed by appealing to humoural medicine: an empty stomach leaves the veins 'unfill'd' and the blood cold and sluggish, making a person irritable and hard-hearted. Once wine and food fill 'these pipes and these conveyances of our blood,' the soul grows 'suppler.' Menenius plans to time his own visit to catch Coriolanus after a good meal, when his body — and his mercy — will be warm.

anchor_text: he does sit in gold, his eye Red as 'twould burn Rome: and his injury The gaoler to his pity
summary: Cominius describes Coriolanus enthroned in gleaming armour — 'sits in gold' — with eyes red as fire, as if his very gaze would set Rome alight. The striking phrase 'his injury the gaoler to his pity' is a metaphor: his wounded pride acts as a jailer that has locked his pity in a cell from which it cannot escape. Pity exists, but rage has imprisoned it.
detail: The image 'sits in gold' sets Coriolanus visually as a remote, kingly figure — appropriate for a man who now commands the Volscian army rather than serving Rome. The 'red eye' carries the double sense of bloodshot anger and of fire: his look matches the burning he intends. The gaoler metaphor is especially precise: it does not say pity is dead, only that it is locked away. This keeps open the dramatic possibility that Volumnia's embassy (foreshadowed at TLN 3055-3058) might unlock it — which is what the play delivers in 5.3. The same pattern of mercy imprisoned by a grievance shapes the structural arc of the final act.

The gaoler metaphor ('his injury the gaoler to his pity') is read accurately — pity imprisoned rather than extinguished, keeping open Volumnia's eventual success — and 'sits in gold' as enthroned in gleaming armour is a mainstream reading; the structural observation that 5.3 unlocks what 5.1 shows imprisoned is a defensible dramatic inference, not an over-reading.

anchor_text: it is lots to blanks
summary: 'Lots to blanks' is an Elizabethan betting phrase meaning 'overwhelming odds in favor' — a lottery had many blanks (losing tickets) and few lots (winning tickets), so 'lots to blanks' inverts the ratio: near-certain odds. Menenius is saying it is almost a sure thing that Coriolanus has mentioned his name.
detail: The phrase is equivalent to the modern 'odds-on' or 'sure bet.' Lotteries were a familiar Elizabethan institution; the government ran one as early as 1567 to finance harbor repairs. Menenius, characteristically, reaches for a witty, familiar image even under pressure.

anchor_text: Like to a bowl upon a subtle ground, I have tumbled past the throw
summary: Menenius uses the game of bowls as a metaphor: a 'subtle' (tricky, uneven) green causes the bowl to overrun the target. He is saying that in praising Coriolanus he sometimes got so carried away that he rolled past the truth into exaggeration. 'Stamp'd the leasing' in the next line means he nearly put a seal of approval on outright lies.
detail: Bowls was the most popular English lawn game of the period, played on a biased bowl on a grass surface; 'subtle ground' describes a green with hidden slopes that deflect the bowl. The verb 'tumbled past the throw' means overshot the jack (target). 'Leasing' is an archaic word for lying (from Old English 'leas,' false); 'stamp'd the leasing' means nearly authenticated a falsehood — as a seal stamps authority on a document. The whole passage is a self-deprecating confession that Menenius is Coriolanus's loyal spin-doctor.

anchor_text: in a violent popular ignorance, given your enemy your shield
summary: The Volscian guard is summarizing what the Roman citizens did: in a burst of mob fury ('violent popular ignorance') they banished the very man who had defended them, handing their own shield to their enemy. 'Popular' here means 'of the common people,' not simply 'widely liked.' This echoes the play's central indictment — that the tribunes stirred the crowd to expel Rome's best soldier.
detail: The phrase 'popular ignorance' encapsulates the play's conservative political argument (drawn from Plutarch) that the mob's emotional volatility makes it an unreliable source of political authority. A 'shield' was a standard emblem of defense and military protection. The guard's analysis is ironic: a Volscian enemy is delivering the most precise and damning account of Rome's political self-destruction. Plutarch's Life of Coriolanus frames the banishment as a catastrophic democratic error; North's 1579 translation was Shakespeare's primary source.

anchor_text: palsied intercession of such a decayed dotant
summary: 'Palsied' means trembling with palsy (paralysis), an old person's shaking. 'Dotant' (also 'dotard') means a senile old man whose mind has softened with age. The guard is brutally mocking Menenius as a shaky, feeble-minded old man whose pleading can no more put out Coriolanus's fire than a dotard's breath can blow out a furnace.

'Dotant' appears rarely in Shakespeare and is based on 'dote' (to be weakly fond, or to be stupefied by age). The Folio text has 'dotant'; some editors emend to 'dotard,' but both mean the same thing. The cumulative list of the frail ('old women... daughters... decayed dotant') serves the rhetorical figure of climax-by-diminution.

summary: A 'jack' was a contemptuous term for a low-born fellow or insolent menial — equivalent to calling someone a 'lackey' or 'nobody.' 'Guardant' means a guard standing on duty (from the heraldic term for an animal shown face-forward). Menenius is sneering at the guard: a mere nobody standing watch cannot use his official role ('office' used as a verb, meaning to use one's office against someone) to block access to his son Coriolanus.

The term 'jack' (low fellow) appears repeatedly in Shakespeare as patrician contempt for the lower orders, and its use here is doubly pointed: Menenius, himself a patrician and Coriolanus's friend, is performing exactly the class contempt that defines the play's world.

anchor_text: The glorious gods sit in hourly synod about thy particular prosperity
summary: A 'synod' was an assembly or council; Menenius imagines the Roman gods convening continuously ('hourly') just to look after Coriolanus's personal welfare. The image is both affectionate and ironic: Menenius heaps divine attention on Coriolanus even as he is being coldly turned away.

Applying the word 'synod' (a formal assembly, the same word used for church councils) to the divine council of Olympus is a familiar classical trope; it frames the gods as a Roman senate in the sky. Menenius's warmth here — calling himself Coriolanus's 'old father' in the next line — makes the subsequent rejection by Coriolanus ('Away!') land all the harder. In Plutarch's account, Menenius is one of the two envoys Coriolanus refuses before his mother succeeds.

anchor_text: Wife, mother, child, I know not. My affairs Are servanted to others
summary: Coriolanus dismisses his entire family in a single brutal catalogue — wife, mother, child — as if they no longer exist for him. The verb 'servanted' (made a servant) is coined on the spot: his will and purposes now belong to the Volscians. The compressed, staccato rhythm of the list ('Wife, mother, child') enacts the finality of the cutting-off.

Coriolanus reverses the expected emotional hierarchy: the more intimate the tie, the more completely he repudiates it. The neologism 'servanted' gives his will over to the Volscians as if he has enslaved his own agency — an inversion of his defining patrician pride. This moment anticipates the turning point in 5.3, when Volumnia, Virgilia, and Young Marcius all appear in person and he cannot hold the same resolve. Plutarch notes that Coriolanus was visibly moved by his mother's presence even when trying not to be.

anchor_text: my remission lies In Volscian breasts
summary: 'Remission' here means the power to pardon or forgive, not the modern medical sense. Coriolanus is saying that although he personally owns the right to take revenge on Rome ('my revenge properly'), the power to grant mercy for Rome sits entirely with the Volscians — his new masters. He has signed away even his capacity for forgiveness.
detail: 'Remission' derives from Latin 'remittere,' to send back or release. In Shakespeare's period it commonly meant pardon or release from an obligation (as in 'remission of sins'). Coriolanus's formulation is legally precise: the syntax distinguishes between owning the right to revenge (which is personal property) and the power of remission (which he has transferred to Volscian authority as part of his new allegiance). The twinned contrast — 'my revenge properly' versus 'my remission lies / In Volscian breasts' — is exactly the kind of cold legal abstraction that defines Coriolanus's self-remaking.

anchor_text: You keep a constant temper.
summary: Aufidius's final line is deliberately ambiguous. 'Temper' means both emotional state (he keeps his feelings constant, unmoved) and the quality of tempered metal (hard, unyielding). Aufidius may be admiring Coriolanus's self-control — or quietly noting, for his own purposes, that the man who refused his oldest friend is also the man he will use and then destroy.
detail: In Plutarch's account, Aufidius has already decided that Coriolanus is a liability and plans to remove him once the war ends. His observation here — the only thing he says in the entire scene — is the cool appraisal of a calculating rival: he is watching Coriolanus demonstrate the inflexibility that will eventually give Aufidius his pretext. The metallurgical meaning of 'temper' (the hardening process applied to metal blades) resonates with the play's persistent warrior-as-iron imagery. An audience who knows the ending hears Aufidius logging a weakness: a man who cannot bend will break.

anchor_text: Nay, godded me indeed
summary: 'Godded' is a coinage meaning 'made a god of,' 'worshipped as divine.' Coriolanus says Menenius loved him so excessively that the old man treated him as a deity rather than a man. The word appears nowhere else in Shakespeare.
detail: The coinage registers the play's running interest in how Rome projects divine honour onto its warrior. Elsewhere the people shout 'He is their god' (5.4) and compare him to an engine or 'thing made for Alexander' (5.4). Coriolanus himself has used the same inflation: he cannot stoop to beg 'voices' from the people because that deference would unmake the godlike autonomy his whole self-image requires. North's Plutarch speaks of the soldiers 'marvelling and wondering' at Marcius as if at a prodigy, and the play converts that awe into theological language.

anchor_text: the honour'd mould Wherein this trunk was fram'd
summary: 'Mould' here means the shape or form in which something is cast — Coriolanus calls Volumnia the honoured clay in which his body ('this trunk') was formed. 'Trunk' means the body as a physical container, as opposed to the soul. The image is of a man shaped by his mother's body the way a statue is shaped by its mould.
detail: The casting metaphor is precise: a mould is impressed from without; once the shape is poured and set, the mould is discarded. The word choice quietly raises a question the scene will answer — can the man survive if he breaks from the form that made him? 'Trunk' for the body is standard early modern usage (OED s.v. 'trunk' 4b) and implies a container that houses the soul, not the whole self.

Coriolanus is saying that Virgilia's tender gaze has the power to unmake his vow not to hear Rome's petition — a power so great it could make even immortal gods perjure themselves.

anchor_text: Be such a gosling to obey instinct; but stand, As if a man were author of himself
summary: A 'gosling' is a young goose — a creature that follows its mother instinctively with no will of its own. Coriolanus is furiously resisting the pull of family feeling by calling it mere animal instinct: a gosling follows its parent because it cannot help it, not from reason. He wants to stand 'as if a man were author of himself' — self-created, owing nothing to parent or nature.
detail: The gosling image is deliberately humiliating: Coriolanus the invincible warrior pictures himself as a baby bird helplessly waddling after its mother if he yields. 'Author of himself' is the play's sharpest statement of his impossible ideal of pure autonomy — to be one's own origin, self-made, free of all bond. The idea is immediately undercut: he is about to yield in exactly the way he boasts he will not. Shakespeare places this as the last wall before the breach, making the fall the more complete.

anchor_text: Like a dull actor now, I have forgot my part and I am out
summary: Coriolanus compares himself to a bad actor who has gone 'out' — lost his lines on stage — and stands humiliated in front of the audience. 'Out' was the technical word for an actor who had forgotten his part. The irony is sharp: the man who despises performance, who refused to 'perform' the consulship ritual, now confesses that genuine emotion has robbed him of all self-command.
detail: The actor-simile is one of the play's central conceits. Volumnia has lectured Coriolanus on playing a role — 'I prithee now, my son, / Go to them with this bonnet in thy hand' (3.2) — and the tribunes have manipulated him by stage-managing the crowd's reaction. He has always refused to perform. Now, when he most needs to maintain a part, emotion dissolves it. The reversal is the scene's deepest irony: he is 'out' not from incompetence but from love.

anchor_text: by the jealous queen of heaven, that kiss I carried from thee
summary: The 'jealous queen of heaven' is Juno, Roman queen of the gods and goddess of marriage — 'jealous' because she was famously vigilant in guarding the fidelity of marriage bonds, and quick to punish those who violated them. Coriolanus swears by her as the goddess most apt to witness the fidelity of a husband's parting kiss, kept pure through years of exile.
detail: In Roman religion Juno Pronuba was the goddess who presided over marriage and bound the married pair together. Her jealousy — most famously displayed in her persecution of Jupiter's lovers — made her the fitting guarantor of marital constancy. Coriolanus's oath is not casual: he invokes the highest guardian of the marriage oath to witness that he has been faithful ('my true lip / Hath virgin'd it e'er since'). The verb 'virgin'd' (a Shakespeare coinage meaning 'kept virginally chaste') makes the claim absolute.

Juno as the jealous guardian of marriage oaths is accurate Roman theology, and the 'virgin'd' coinage reading (virginal chastity of the kiss preserved through exile) is supported directly by the text at TLN 3215; the invocation as witness to marital fidelity is the natural reading.

anchor_text: let the pebbles on the hungry beach Fillip the stars; then let the mutinous winds Strike the proud cedars 'gainst the fiery sun
summary: Coriolanus piles up three images of things that cannot happen: beach pebbles flicking ('filliping') the stars, winds driving trees into the sun. 'Fillip' means to strike with a flick of the finger. All three images describe the same idea — if his mother bowing to him made sense, then impossible things would have to be true. This is the rhetorical figure of adynaton, piling up impossibilities to say 'never.'
detail: Adynaton (the 'I would sooner...' formula) was a standard figure of classical oratory and poetry. The images here are each technically precise: beach pebbles are the lowest and lightest things; the stars, remotest. Cedars were the tallest trees of antiquity (used in Ezekiel, Virgil, and Ovid as emblems of pride); the fiery sun is above even them. The 'hungry beach' (a beach that consumes ships, that longs for wrecks) is the more startling epithet — it gives the sea a predator's appetite before the impossibility stacks on top. The whole passage is Shakespeare's amplification of a much shorter moment in Plutarch.

Coriolanus blesses his young son in the language of a soldier, praying that the war gods will 'inform' (fill, breathe into) the boy's mind with nobleness — a military, god-given virtue rather than a domestic one.

anchor_text: capitulate Again with Rome's mechanics
summary: 'Capitulate' here means to negotiate or to treat with (someone) under articles — it does not mean to surrender; it means to come to terms by drawing up conditions chapter by chapter (from Latin 'caput,' a chapter or heading). 'Mechanics' means manual workers, craftsmen, the labouring class. Coriolanus refuses to negotiate again with Rome's working people — the very citizens whose 'voices' he could not bring himself to beg for the consulship.
detail: The root of 'capitulate' is the Latin 'capitulum' (a little head, a chapter or article of an agreement); to capitulate was to draw up conditions in chapters, hence to treat or parley. Its modern sense of surrender came later; Shakespeare always uses it to mean 'negotiate terms.' 'Mechanics' (from Greek 'mechane,' a tool or contrivance) was a standard Elizabethan contemptuous term for those who work with their hands — artisans, tradesmen — as opposed to gentlemen or soldiers. The word choice marks Coriolanus's class contempt even in his refusal.

anchor_text: our raiment And state of bodies would bewray what life We have led
summary: 'Bewray' means to reveal or betray (a secret or hidden truth), usually without the subject intending to. Volumnia says that even if she said nothing, her mourning clothes and her worn, grief-aged body would involuntarily disclose the suffering they have lived through since Coriolanus's exile. The word is archaic even in Shakespeare's day, already being replaced by 'betray.'
detail: The root is Old English 'wregan,' to accuse or expose. 'State of bodies' means the visible condition of their bodies — their thinness, paleness, the marks of grief. Volumnia's point is rhetorically shrewd: she will not need arguments if the visual fact of their suffering speaks first. The speech begins its long appeal with silence and bare appearance before escalating through logic and emotional pressure.

anchor_text: The son, the husband, and the father, tearing His country's bowels out
summary: 'Bowels' in Elizabethan usage meant the inward parts, but also — by extension — the deepest seat of feeling or pity (as in 'bowels of mercy'). Here Volumnia uses it to mean Rome's vitals: Coriolanus is tearing out the entrails of his own homeland. The image fuses bodily dismemberment with the destruction of the political body, making the attack on Rome literal infanticide carried out by the city's own son.
detail: The body-politic metaphor — Rome as a living body — is the play's governing frame from the opening belly-fable onward (1.1). Volumnia now turns it against her son: he is not merely attacking a city but gutting the body that bore him. 'Bowels' as the seat of compassion ('bowels of mercy') is biblical (Colossians 3:12 Geneva: 'the bowels of mercies') as well as physiological; the word's double valence (entrails and compassionate depth) presses Coriolanus from both sides at once — he is both destroying and displaying an absence of mercy.

anchor_text: as a foreign recreant, be led With manacles through our streets
summary: A 'recreant' was a coward, a traitor, or one who had abandoned his faith or allegiance — from Old French 'recroire,' to surrender one's cause. Volumnia presses the logic of his choice: if Coriolanus's Volscian army loses, he will be paraded as a defeated enemy through Roman streets in chains ('manacles' are metal handcuffs or shackles). Either outcome of the battle destroys him.
detail: The word 'recreant' carried its full moral charge: it named someone who cried 'craven' in a trial by combat, surrendering God's judgment against himself, and by extension any traitor to his sworn allegiance. For Coriolanus, who has defined his entire self through martial honour, the vision of being led in chains as a 'foreign recreant' — treated as one of the foreign enemies he has always fought — is the most humiliating possible outcome. Volumnia is systematically closing every exit until the only honourable path is mercy.

anchor_text: bear the palm for having bravely shed Thy wife and children's blood
summary: The palm branch was the classical prize of victory, awarded to athletes, generals, and conquerors — 'bearing the palm' means winning the greatest prize, being the champion. Volumnia twists the image: if Coriolanus conquers Rome, his 'trophy' will be the blood of his own family. The victor's wreath becomes a mark of horror, not honour.
detail: The palm of victory descends from Greco-Roman athletic and military tradition; Roman triumphs were celebrated with laurel and palm. Volumnia's rhetoric is carefully constructed: she grants Coriolanus his cherished categories (valour, bravery, triumph) and then fills them with the worst possible content — a triumph whose captives are his own wife and children. The move is formally an antistrophe (repeating a term in an altered meaning), turning the language of glory into an indictment.

anchor_text: Thou hast affected the fine strains of honour, To imitate the graces of the gods, To tear with thunder the wide cheeks o' the air
summary: 'Affected' means desired or pursued. 'Strains' means qualities or tendencies — the fine strains of honour are its highest, most refined characteristics. Volumnia turns his own aspirations against him: he has always tried to be godlike in honour, to thunder like Jove — and then she points out he is 'charging his sulphur with a bolt that should but rive an oak' — spending divine force on something beneath it. 'Rive' means to split or tear apart.
detail: The passage is Volumnia's most powerful rhetorical move: she does not argue against his values but shows him he is violating them. 'Tear with thunder the wide cheeks o' the air' evokes Jupiter's thunderbolt — the weapon of supreme divine power. 'Sulphur' is the ancient name for the material in lightning. To use a thunderbolt to split an oak, rather than to do something worthy of it, is to waste divine power on a petty act. The implication: destroying Rome is precisely such a waste of his greatness. The technique is classical: turn the opponent's own standards against them.

anchor_text: I am glad thou hast set thy mercy and thy honour At difference in thee; out of that I'll work Myself a former fortune

anchor_text: throats are sentenced, and stay upon execution

Shakespeare uses similar legal-execution language elsewhere to sharpen a political crisis into something personal and inescapable.

anchor_text: differency between a grub and a butterfly; yet your butterfly was a grub. This Marcius is grown from man to dragon
summary: Menenius uses a metamorphosis image — a caterpillar becoming a butterfly — to argue that transformation does not erase origins. The grub/butterfly becomes a ladder to the more startling claim: Marcius has not merely changed but has become something mythological and monstrous, 'more than a creeping thing.' The progression (grub → butterfly → dragon) escalates each step beyond natural limits.
detail: The rhetorical figure is *gradatio* or climax — a step-by-step ascent through increasingly extreme comparisons. The butterfly conceit was a familiar Elizabethan way of describing social or spiritual metamorphosis; Shakespeare uses it several times (e.g. Troilus and Cressida 3.3.78 'the butterfly Achilles'). Menenius's version inverts it: he first grants Sicinius's implicit point (a man can change), then leaps past it — Marcius's change has gone further than nature allows, into the realm of legend. The dragon, a classical and heraldic symbol of martial terror, frames Coriolanus as no longer human. Plutarch describes Coriolanus's ferocity in similar superlatives in the Life of Coriolanus (North 1579).

anchor_text: A merrier day did never yet greet Rome, No, not the expulsion of the Tarquins
summary: The expulsion of the Tarquins refers to the overthrow of Tarquin the Proud, Rome's last king, in 509 BCE — the event that ended the monarchy and created the Roman Republic. The comparison is charged: a play set in the earliest years of that Republic is now measuring Volumnia's persuasion of her son against the Republic's very birth. That the Messenger names this as the only possible rival to the current joy also measures how close to annihilation Rome has come — the city nearly ended the Republic Tarquin's expulsion created.

anchor_text: trumpets, sackbuts, psalteries, and fifes, Tabors and cymbals
summary: A list of instruments that would have been familiar to an Elizabethan audience: sackbuts are early trombones (large S-shaped brass instruments); psalteries are plucked string instruments like small harps; fifes are small high-pitched flutes; tabors are small drums beaten with a stick. Together they represent the full range of the city's festive noise — brass, strings, woodwind, and percussion.
detail: The sackbut (from French *sacqueboute*, 'pull-push') was the Renaissance precursor of the trombone and was commonly used in civic and church ceremony. The psaltery (from Greek *psalterion*, a stringed instrument) was played by plucking — associated in the Bible with sacred music (Psalm 150, Geneva 1599). Tabors were the standard small drum of street celebration, carried by the same performer who played the pipe (fife). This enumeration is characteristic of Shakespeare's use of *enumeratio* to create an impression of overflowing civic sound — the city itself is the instrument. The stage direction calls for 'trumpets and hautboys' (oboes) as well, making the passage one of the play's most spectacular sonic moments.

anchor_text: patroness, the life of Rome
summary: The First Senator hails Volumnia as Rome's 'patroness' — a formal honorific used for a protector or guardian deity of a city, here applied to a mortal woman who has just saved Rome from her own son's army. The title elevates her to almost divine status, appropriate to Roman civic religion in which the city owed its preservation to divine patrons.

By styling Volumnia 'patroness,' the senator frames her act of persuasion as Rome's salvation — an act of founding-level magnitude. Plutarch's Life of Coriolanus records that the Senate honored the women with public games and granted them whatever they wished; he adds that a temple to Female Fortune ('Fortuna Muliebris') was built on the spot where Volumnia met Coriolanus (Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus, ch. 37, North 1579). Shakespeare condenses that honorific into a single word.

'Stoutness' in early modern English means proud firmness or obstinacy, not physical size.

anchor_text: grace thee with that robbery, thy stol'n name / Coriolanus, in Corioli
summary: Coriolanus's surname was awarded by the Roman general Cominius after he single-handedly stormed the Volscian city of Corioli (Act 1). Aufidius calls it 'stolen' because he insists the name was taken from the Volscians in an act of conquest -- using it in their own city of Antium is an affront. By stripping Coriolanus back to 'Marcius,' Aufidius publicly unmakes the honor that defines him.

anchor_text: like / A twist of rotten silk
summary: Aufidius compares Coriolanus's broken oath to a rotted silk thread -- something that looks strong but snaps instantly under pressure. 'Twist' is a strand of twisted thread or silk cord. The simile is cutting because Coriolanus prided himself on iron constancy; Aufidius reduces his vow to cheap, already-decayed fabric.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'twist', n. 1a: 'A thread or cord formed by twisting together two or more threads or strands.' The image of weak or rotten silk for a broken promise is a common early modern rhetorical figure.

A 'twist' as a strand of cord and the simile of rotten silk for a broken oath that looked strong but snapped instantly are defensible and the irony -- Coriolanus, famed for constancy, accused of fragility -- is plainly operative in the scene.

anchor_text: his fame folds in / This orb o' the earth
summary: 'Folds in' means encompasses or contains, as a cloak wraps around something. 'Orb o' the earth' is the globe itself. The Second Lord is saying that Coriolanus's fame encircles the whole world -- an extreme eulogy delivered at the moment of his murder. 'Orb' could also suggest the celestial sphere of the great-chain cosmology, placing Coriolanus among the highest ranks of earthly beings.

anchor_text: Let him be regarded / As the most noble corse that ever herald / Did follow to his um
summary: 'Corse' is an archaic form of 'corpse.' A herald in Roman and Elizabethan ceremonial was the officer who organized and led solemn processions, including funeral ones. 'Um' (urn) is where ashes of the cremated dead were kept after the Roman funeral rite. The First Lord is ordering that Coriolanus receive the highest military funeral honors the Volscians can give -- the same rite a Roman general would have had.
detail: In Plutarch's account the Volscians gave Coriolanus an honorable burial with public mourning; Shakespeare compresses this into a few lines. The urn-and-herald image invokes Roman funerary practice: a great warrior was cremated, his ashes placed in an urn, and heralds preceded his procession. The First Lord's tribute is significant: even the enemy whose city Coriolanus threatened acknowledges his greatness after death -- a final irony of the de casibus pattern.

anchor_text: Beat thou the drum, that it speak mournfully; / Trail your steel pikes
summary: Trailing (dragging) pikes along the ground was a recognized military funeral gesture in Elizabethan and Roman practice: soldiers lowered their weapons to show grief and submission rather than readiness for battle. A muffled or 'mournful' drum beat a slow pace for a funeral procession. Aufidius's commands signal that the exit will be a formal military cortege despite the chaotic murder that just occurred.
